They do not come from the difficulty of the task or from material limits. Manufactured necessity keeps the institution simple upstream and within budget by pushing coordination work onto users, claimants, or operators.
examples: A state benefit portal requires applicants to repeatedly re-upload identical income verification documents in person because internal databases are not integrated, and frames the friction as an unavoidable fraud-prevention necessity.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes. Ways systems fail to keep capability, authority, evidence, dependency, standing, and correction coupled.
operationalTests: The institution has checked whether a demand on people would disappear if it did the coordination or database reconciliation itself.
The human time a hurdle takes is counted as an operating cost in the program budget.
entries.genealogy: Draws on administrative burden theory (Herd and Moynihan) and public choice critique.

entries.title: Structural coercion
entries.bodyHtml: A condition in which adapting to a defective system is voluntary on paper, but refusing is not a real option. Refusal brings serious harm, system breakdown, or moral sanction. No one issues a command. The coercion runs through dependency, unequal exit costs, and professional norms turned against the people who hold them.
examples: A clinician cannot decline unpaid documentation workarounds, because stopping would endanger patients. Their care for patients becomes an operating subsidy.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes. Ways systems fail to keep capability, authority, evidence, dependency, standing, and correction coupled.
operationalTests: The institution can state what happens, materially and in working relationships, to someone who uses their formal right to refuse an undocumented workaround.
Compliance does not rest on an exit cost that falls only on the less powerful party.
entries.genealogy: Draws on republican political theory (Pettit's non-domination) and feminist care ethics (Tronto, Kittay).

references.label: The human subsidy to institutional continuity

entries.title: Manufactured virtue
entries.bodyHtml: The relabeling of ways of coping with a defective system as personal or professional virtues. When an institution praises workers as “dependable,” “flexible,” or “resilient,” it credits their personality with surviving its own gaps, and it leaves the defect that made the coping necessary in place.
examples: A support engineer is praised as exceptionally “flexible” for answering off-hours escalation alerts caused by an unpatched deployment bug.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes. Ways systems fail to keep capability, authority, evidence, dependency, standing, and correction coupled.
operationalTests: Performance reviews distinguish praise for skill from praise for patching undocumented system defects.
When a praised behavior exists to patch a defect, the defect is logged for repair.
entries.genealogy: Draws on organizational sociology and labor process theory (Burawoy).

references.label: The human subsidy to institutional continuity

entries.title: Epistemic erasure cycle
entries.bodyHtml: A recursive feedback failure where successful human adaptation to a system defect prevents the defect from generating an error signal. Because human competence keeps output within acceptable bounds, telemetry and dashboards report healthy operation, institutional learning is blocked, and the defect is preserved.
examples: In a triage queue, nurses manually reassign misrouted high-priority cases, so the hospital's automated routing algorithm reports zero adverse triage delays.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes. Ways systems fail to keep capability, authority, evidence, dependency, standing, and correction coupled.
operationalTests: Error rates are measured during work-to-rule periods, and a rise is read as the defect showing itself.
Dashboard metrics register a signal when frontline workarounds spike.
entries.genealogy: Draws on cybernetic feedback theory (Wiener, Ashby) and the theory essay on absorption as concealment.

references.label: The human subsidy to institutional continuity

entries.title: Exhaustion-biased instrument
entries.bodyHtml:
An instrument whose readings improve as the people it observes run down. A survey, an appeal, a complaint log, and a self-assessment all draw their input from the subject's remaining attention, so the depleted answer least and the institution reads the gap as health. The bias runs one direction: more depletion produces a better-looking reading.

Law VIII asks whether an observation can change the governing state of a system. This asks the prior question, whether the observation is evidence at all. An instrument bought with the subject's last reserves has a sampling rule that ties difficulty to silence.

It co-occurs with attrition-as-resolution and endurance asymmetry. The remedy is to read friction from the system's own trail — abandonment at a named step, re-uploads, retries, activity outside scheduled hours — rather than to ask a depleted person to describe it.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Recurring ways responsibility dissolves, authority drifts from its evidence, and harm lands on people with no route to challenge it.
examples: A jurisdiction reports 4% appeal volume and a 96% resolution rate in the same quarter it adds a second documentation requirement. The appeals that stopped arriving appear in neither figure.

entries.title: Score as acquittal
entries.bodyHtml:
An anti-pattern where a metric is treated as settling a question it was built to inform. A burden ratio, a friction budget, a safety-case result, or a diagnostic score records what an instrument observed; it does not establish that the person affected is wrong. Citing a passing score against an objection converts a measurement into a verdict, and the verdict is reached by a party that did not have to live the outcome being measured.

STD-02 §5.4 holds that a measurement the challenged party did not produce is evidence and not a bar. Where a score and an account conflict, the conflict goes to a named reviewer holding authority to resolve it.

It is the technocratic failure mode that exhaustion-biased instrument enables from the other side. That term covers an instrument that under-reports because collecting it cost the subject. This one covers an instrument that is accurate and is then cited as though accuracy ended the argument. An instrument can be well built and still be the wrong authority.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Recurring ways responsibility dissolves, authority drifts from its evidence, and harm lands on people with no route to challenge it.
examples: A deployment reports a burden ratio of 6.8 against a ceiling of 7.2, and an operator's account of how long a form actually takes is closed on that basis.

entries.title: Unwired evidence
entries.bodyHtml:
Evidence an institution holds that no rule obliges it to act on. The list of review triggers on a policy record is written by the institution, and it can be narrower than what the institution knows: the clinical service has adopted the new guideline, the specialist wrote the paper, the committee it staffs published the revision — and the coverage rule runs as if none of it arrived. The knowledge exists. The wiring between it and the rule does not.

It differs from non-conversion in what is being refused. That term covers capability converting itself into authority without a decision. This one covers evidence converting into nothing at all: no status change, no reconsideration, no review — because the class of evidence was never declared, and declaring it is the institution's own choice.

It is the mechanism behind the outdated rulebook: guidance that stays years behind the science not because the science was unknown but because the office that knows is not the office the rule reads. STD-08 §2.7 closes it by making the holding of evidence itself a fired trigger — the clock runs from the day the evidence was held, not the day someone upstairs was told.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Recurring ways responsibility dissolves, authority drifts from its evidence, and harm lands on people with no route to challenge it.
examples: A health plan's medical policy cites a 2021 criterion for an imaging study while the specialty society replaced it in 2024; three of the plan's own network physicians are authors of the replacement.

entries.title: Automation bias
entries.bodyHtml:
The tendency to accept an automated output in place of the judgment it was supposed to support. It is strongest exactly when the operator has the least capacity to resist it: late in a shift, under volume, when the output is plausible and fluent and appears in a queue that looks pre-screened. The operator glances, assumes the system reconciled the labs, and signs.

It matters because it converts a queuing defect into an incident. A system that places a dangerous order into a routine signing queue is relying on a person to catch it, and a person at the end of a shift catches it less and less often. The failure is not carelessness; it is the predictable response of a finite operator to a plausible draft. That is why the control is structural and not exhortative: a synchronous hard stop that requires a documented rationale before the order exists works regardless of how tired the operator is, while a reminder to "pay attention" does not.

Law IX already states the shape: human oversight is a control only if the human can alter system state. Automation bias names the load that oversight is placed under, and intervention specification is what the control looks like when it is designed for the tired operator rather than the attentive one.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Recurring ways responsibility dissolves, authority drifts from its evidence, and harm lands on people with no route to challenge it.
examples: An order set auto-populates with a home medication despite an acute creatinine jump, and sits in a batch the physician reviews at the end of a fourteen-hour shift.

entries.title: Operator instrumentation
entries.bodyHtml:
Instrumenting the person operating a system — gaze tracking, keystroke dynamics, dwell-speed measurement, continuous attention scoring — to detect the burden the system imposes. It fails for the same reason every other measurement that watches the person fails: under management incentives, a metric of human effort becomes a quota of human effort. The instrument built to prove the system is exhausting its operators is repurposed to rank them, and the operators learn to perform calm for the sensor, which destroys the signal it was installed to capture.

The boundary it violates: containment audits the state transitions of the machine, never the nervous system of the operator. The machine's trail — non-attributable aggregates of queue depth, retry counts, and rework volume — can indicate system burden without identifying or ranking an operator. Reading the trail is the exhaustion-biased instrument answered correctly: system-state evidence that does not identify the person. The audit burden ceiling caps what may be asked of a respondent; this boundary caps what may be observed of them.

The line is not that human experience is unmeasurable. It is who measures and what the measurement is for. Self-reported instruments — the operator reporting their own load — are the person's evidence about the system and belong to them. Machine-instrumented behavioral telemetry is the institution's evidence about the person, and it converts every protective metric it produces into a performance instrument the moment incentives favor it. Compensated performance is what the telemetry was built to find; a quota is what it becomes.

The theory essay on the sovereign override carries the design consequence: the machine boundary is deterministic and watches records; the human boundary is sovereign and is watched by nothing, because a boundary that watches the operator becomes the next control system.
entries.scope: B. Failure modes (why Ethotechnics exists). Recurring ways responsibility dissolves, authority drifts from its evidence, and harm lands on people with no route to challenge it.
examples: A burnout dashboard built from keystroke cadence and after-hours activity is quietly repointed at the slowest decile of clinicians the quarter after staffing falls short.

categories.heading: C. What a system must be able to do
categories.descriptionHtml: What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.

entries.title: Stoppability
entries.bodyHtml:
A system's ability to halt harmful processes quickly, safely, and deliberately, without requiring heroism or escalation. It needs automatic halts that fire on signs of harm, a target for time to halt that is measured, and operators with clear authority to stop.

Stop paths are rehearsed, observable, and usable under stress, and do not sit behind exceptional permissions.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: Each high-risk workflow has documented stop controls, owners, and on-call coverage.
Time-to-halt targets are met during drills or real incidents, with outcomes logged.
entries.genealogy: Adapts safety-engineering stop controls to harm to people and to accountability for it.
examples: A dispatch platform can pause automated routing citywide within minutes when false-priority signals spike, while preserving manual override for emergency coordinators.

entries.title: Reversibility
entries.bodyHtml: Critical actions can be undone and people restored to a safe prior state. Damage is not permanent by default, and time-to-restore stays low.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: Critical actions have tested rollback or remediation paths that restore data and access.
Time-to-restore targets are met during drills and documented in the repair log.
entries.genealogy: Applies rollback discipline to consequences for people as well as to technical failures.

minimumEvidence.artifact: Documented rollback plan with owners, restoration steps, and eligibility criteria for reversals.
minimumEvidence.behavior: Reversal executed during drills or incidents with people restored to their prior state.
minimumEvidence.metric: Time-to-restore targets tracked and met across reversal events.

entries.title: Fair burden distribution
entries.bodyHtml:
Failures should not fall hardest on the most vulnerable. Fair burden distribution treats time, cost, stress, and procedural labor as design variables and tracks them with measures like the user burden ratio.

When burden concentrates on people with the least capacity to absorb it, systems must rebalance defaults, staffing, and escalation pathways.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
examples: A benefits workflow waives redundant verification for applicants with prior validated records instead of repeatedly requesting the same documents.

entries.title: Contestability
entries.bodyHtml:
A person affected by a decision can challenge it, and the challenge can change the outcome.

It has four parts and needs all four: standing, meaning a named party may raise the challenge; a channel that receives it; an obliged responder who must answer on a clock against a stated standard; and a state change the challenge is capable of producing. Three of the four is a complaints process. The apparatus that supplies them is a standing mechanism, and the fourth part is what gives a challenge procedural force rather than a reply.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: Appeals route to reviewers with authority to overturn outcomes.
Appeal passage rate and response time are tracked and used to improve decisions.
Appeal outcomes are recorded as overturns, restorations, or policy changes, never only as “review completed.”
An appeal passage rate below 5% for 30 days triggers a redesign review.
The share of appeals that produce a decision artifact is tracked and published.
entries.genealogy: Draws from due process norms so people can challenge and reverse harm.

entries.title: Explainability for accountability
entries.bodyHtml: Explanations a person can act on, not decorative ones. They identify the decision owner, the data or policy basis, and how the outcome can be corrected, enabling contestability and audits. Explainability for accountability is legibility plus a working correction path.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: Decision notices include the reason, data source, owner, and path to contest.
Explanations are tested with affected people for whether they understand them and can act on them.
entries.genealogy: Moves explainability from transparency theater to accountability and repair.

entries.title: Refusal-tolerant systems
entries.bodyHtml: The system remains usable when people opt out, are confused, make mistakes, or withdraw cooperation. Refusal tolerance prevents extraction by endurance by treating refusal as a valid input, not a failure state. Called “human” because it protects humans from being turned into the crumple zone when they refuse.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: Opt-out or decline flows keep core services available without punitive delays.
Manual alternatives are staffed and tooled so refusals do not create hidden labor.
entries.genealogy: Centers refusal as a valid form of agency within system design.

entries.title: Graceful degradation
entries.bodyHtml: The system sheds features or load in controlled stages while keeping people safe. It keeps baseline commitments such as live support and data export, keeps the system stoppable, and keeps the time to restore people short.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.

entries.title: Soft edges
entries.bodyHtml: Boundary conditions designed to cushion people instead of penalizing them — graduated responses, warnings before lockouts, and reversible defaults. They reduce the harm done when the system fails and keep it from breaking under ordinary variation.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: Users receive warnings and reversible options before thresholds or lockouts.
Escalation steps are graduated with safe fallbacks instead of hard failures.
entries.genealogy: Applies the graduated responses of safety design to reduce failure load and brittleness.

entries.title: Governability
entries.bodyHtml: The degree to which a system can be steered, paused, audited, corrected, or shut down after deployment. It is high only when the system can be stopped, its actions can be undone, and its decisions stay open to challenge.
examples: The city’s benefits system can be paused, rolled back, and audited within hours.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.

entries.title: Incident literacy
entries.bodyHtml: The ability to recognize failures as incidents (not anomalies) and respond with containment, logging, escalation, and repair. It combines automatic halts with a repair record kept up to date.
examples: A moderation team opens an incident ticket for bias spikes instead of filing a bug report.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.

entries.title: Capability discovery
entries.bodyHtml:
The practice of finding out what an assembled decision system can do, including reachable tools, side effects, and action classes nobody intended to expose. Discovery is testing and cataloging, and its output is a capability catalog rather than a permission.

It matters because capability that has not been discovered can be neither authorized nor refused. Keeping discovery separate from authorization is how a new capability stays outside the authority grant until someone decides it belongs there.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: Discovery runs against the assembled system, including tools reachable through chained calls.
Discovery output is written to the catalog and never directly to a grant.
The harness confirms that a newly discovered capability is refused at execution until granted.
entries.genealogy: Operationalizes Law I by making discovery a first-class activity whose result is knowledge, not permission.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A discovery run report listing reachable action classes and how each was verified.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A discovered but ungranted capability refused at execution and logged.
minimumEvidence.metric: Interval since the last discovery run per decision system.

entries.title: Correction capacity
entries.bodyHtml:
The measured ability to intervene: which interventions exist, who may invoke them, how long they take, and how much load the institution can absorb while they run. Capacity is counted in people, clocks, and rehearsals rather than asserted in a policy.

It matters because a correction obligation with no matching capacity is a promise the institution cannot keep. Capacity is also perishable, losing ground to capacity depreciation unless it is replenished, and its detection component counts for nothing without evaluation independence. Capacity is the quantity that must grow alongside delegated agency, and it is the property an evaluation layer above the model is needed to test.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: Every stated intervention has a named invoker, a measured time to effect, and a last-exercised date.
Capacity is compared against authority at each expansion review, not only at launch.
Interventions never exercised within a stated interval are treated as unproven.
entries.genealogy: Turns Law IV from a duty into a measurement: correction capacity is what the institution can demonstrate, not what it intends.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An intervention inventory with invokers, time to effect, and last-exercised dates.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An intervention exercised in a drill within its stated time to effect.
minimumEvidence.metric: Ratio of authorized action volume to demonstrated correction throughput.

entries.title: Technical reversibility
entries.bodyHtml:
The mechanism for undoing an action exists and works. The switch throws, the rollback completes, the state restores, and a test proves it on the version of the system currently running. It is the first of three levels of reversibility.

It matters as a floor rather than a finding. Technical reversibility is the cheapest of the three levels to claim and the least informative, because a working switch says nothing about whether operational reversibility or institutional reversibility would survive it being thrown.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: The rollback path is exercised against the current build, not a past one.
Restore completeness is measured, including derived state and downstream caches.
A failed rollback test blocks release rather than producing a follow-up ticket.
entries.genealogy: The first rung of the Law VI ladder, kept separate so a passing technical test cannot be reported as reversibility.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A rollback test report against the current build, with restore completeness measured.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A rollback executed in a drill that restored state without manual repair.
minimumEvidence.metric: Rollback success rate and time to restore, per release.

entries.title: Operational reversibility
entries.bodyHtml:
The people and processes around a system can absorb a correction once it is made. Staff know the fallback, queues can hold the load, and the manual path has been exercised recently enough to work. It is the second of three levels of reversibility.

It matters because most corrections fail here rather than at the switch. Operational reversibility is what a withdrawal rehearsal measures, and its absence turns technical reversibility into a claim nobody will test during an incident.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: The fallback path has been run with real volume within a stated interval.
Staffing for the fallback is costed and available, not notional.
Backlog accumulated during a rehearsal is measured and shown to be recoverable.
entries.genealogy: The second rung of the Law VI ladder, where the question moves from the mechanism to the people who must live through its use.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A rehearsal report showing the fallback carrying real work for a stated period.
minimumEvidence.behavior: Frontline staff executing the manual path without escalation during a drill.
minimumEvidence.metric: Backlog accumulated per hour of fallback operation, and time to clear it.

entries.title: Institutional reversibility
entries.bodyHtml:
The organization running a system can survive having made a correction to it. Commitments, contracts, reputations, and budgets all remain serviceable after withdrawal. It is the third of three levels of reversibility, above technical and operational reversibility.

It matters because a correction that would cause unacceptable damage will not be exercised, and an unexercisable correction is not a control. Institutional reversibility is the level that dependency state erodes and that preserved capacity is maintained to defend.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: The institutional consequences of withdrawal are written down, owned, and priced.
At least one senior owner can state what withdrawal would cost without preparing a paper.
Contracts and public commitments are reviewed for terms that make withdrawal unaffordable.
entries.genealogy: The third rung of the Law VI ladder and the level Law XII protects, since a system may draw on institutional capacity but may not consume it.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A withdrawal impact assessment covering contracts, commitments, and budget.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A withdrawal decision taken and survived, or a rehearsal that priced it credibly.
minimumEvidence.metric: Estimated institutional cost of withdrawal, trended against exposure score.

entries.title: Intervention specification
entries.bodyHtml:
A statement of who may intervene in an automated process, on what signal, with what information, with authority over which state, on what timescale, and what happens when they disagree. It replaces “human in the loop” as the name of a control.

It matters because a role is not a control. Naming a human is compatible with that human being unable to alter anything, which is why oversight clauses resolve to an intervention specification and to meaningful control rather than to a named human alone, and why its absence shows up as rubber-stamp review.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: Each oversight clause resolves to a specification answering all six questions.
The specification names a state the human can alter, not only a decision they can approve.
A disagreement path exists and has been exercised at least once.
entries.genealogy: Retires “human in the loop” as a control name and gives Law IX a testable object.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An intervention specification per oversight point, with signal, information, authority, and clock.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A human intervention that altered system state, traced end to end.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of oversight points with a complete specification, and interventions exercised per quarter.

entries.title: Prospective auditability
entries.bodyHtml:
Designing a system so that the questions an audit will ask can be answered later, by recording evidence, authority, and reasoning at the time of each decision rather than reconstructing them afterward. It is decided at build time and cannot be retrofitted onto decisions already made.

It matters because retrospective audits mostly discover that the record does not exist. Prospective auditability is what makes a consequential decision reviewable at all, and it is why a policy record is written before it is needed rather than assembled during an inquiry.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: The audit question set is written before launch and each question maps to a recorded field.
A sample decision from last quarter can be fully reconstructed from records alone.
Missing fields block release rather than becoming audit findings a year later.
entries.genealogy: Inverts the audit relationship: instead of auditing what was kept, the system keeps what will be audited.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An audit question set mapped to recorded fields, dated before launch.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A past decision reconstructed from records without contacting the owning team.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of audit questions answerable from records alone, sampled quarterly.

entries.title: Evaluation independence
entries.bodyHtml:
The property that no single provider is necessary to both execute a consequential process and evaluate it. Execution and evaluation may be bought in the same market, but the institution must still be able to run the evaluation when the executing provider withdraws, degrades, or disputes the result.

A system that grades its own homework has no detection component, however much telemetry it emits, so detection is not satisfied by instrumentation the executing provider alone supplies or controls, and the evaluator has to be named. The property is carried by authority_grant.correction_capacity.detection.independent_of_executor and dependency_record.independent_evaluation, and bound by STD-08 §4.6.

It matters because detection is the first component of correction capacity, and a dependence that captures detection removes correction while leaving the diagram intact. Independence is the part of dependency state that substitution cost alone will not show, since an institution can afford to replace a provider and still be unable to check one.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: For each consequential process, the executing provider and the evaluating party are named separately, and the evaluator can report while the executor disputes the finding.
Detection signals are reproducible from a source the executing provider does not supply or control.
The evaluation has been run in a rehearsal with the executing provider's own telemetry withheld.
entries.genealogy: Extends the Law X evaluation stack to the provider: a layer above the model is only a layer if someone other than the executor can run it.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A grant record whose detection component names an evaluator independent of the executor, matched by the dependency record's independent_evaluation entry.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An evaluation completed and reported while the executing provider's telemetry was unavailable or contested.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential processes whose execution and evaluation do not depend on one provider.

entries.title: Exception learning
entries.bodyHtml:
The modification of a system by its own exceptions: a recurring failure changes the rule, category, workflow, or authority that produced it. It is the counterpart of exception absorption, which handles each case and changes nothing.

It matters because most contestability regimes measure whether a case was resolved, which is the weaker capacity. Exception learning is measured by whether the failure changed the evidentiary rule, the ontology, the authority, or the allocation of burden. The deepest Ethotechnic sequence runs residual → signal → standing → correction → institutional revision, and only the final step is learning.

The capacity this process exercises is structural corrigibility: repeated failures can modify the machinery that produces them. A system with excellent appeals and no mechanism by which appeals alter upstream design has corrected cases and changed nothing about the delegation.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: A recurring exception changes a policy, category, workflow, or authority object, not only the case.
An aggregated exception pattern reaches a review trigger and produces a decision.
The institution can name the last exception that changed an upstream rule.
entries.genealogy: The capability the casebook's learning-outcome verdict scores, argued for in the theory of exception learning.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A rule, category, or authority object whose state history shows changes triggered by exception patterns.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A challenge volume feeding a policy review and changing the policy's state.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of exception classes that produced an upstream object change.

entries.title: Case corrigibility
entries.bodyHtml:
The capacity to fix a particular bad decision: an appeal is heard, a reversal is issued, a person is restored. It is what most contestability regimes measure, because it is what the instruments can see.

It matters because case corrigibility without structural corrigibility is locally corrigible and globally rigid: the person is restored, the pattern is not, and everything the institution does about the pattern happens after the fact and at the level of the individual, which is the one level at which the pattern does not appear.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: A contested decision can be reversed by a named authority within a declared clock.
The reversal is recorded and the person is restored to their prior state.
Case-level reversals are counted separately from changes to the upstream rule.
entries.genealogy: Half of the corrigibility distinction the theory of exception learning draws; the other half is structural corrigibility.

entries.title: Institutional learning
entries.bodyHtml:
Learning that changes what an institution is permitted to do, as distinct from what a model predicts. The model retrains and the prediction improves, while the appeal never changes the evidentiary rule and the exception never changes the ontology; that is model learning without institutional learning.

It matters because Ethotechnics cares about the second. The test is political: did the failure alter the evidentiary rule, redistribute authority, change who pays for the burden, or constrain what the institution may do next time? If not, the machine may be learning while the institution remains structurally unchanged. See also exception learning.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: A failure that changed no policy, authority, or burden allocation is not reported as learning.
Retraining and workflow optimization are distinguished from changes to evidentiary rules or authority.
The institution can name what a past failure is now entitled to constrain.
entries.genealogy: Distinguishes the learning Ethotechnics requires from the learning model vendors report.

entries.title: Corrective debt
entries.bodyHtml:
The accumulated gap between an institution's capacity to act and its capacity to detect, contest, reverse, and repair its errors. As action capacity compounds — more data sources integrated, more decisions automated, more downstream consumers, more dependence — while correction machinery stays fixed, corrective debt grows even if no policy document changes.

It matters because it is the historical form of the Ethotechnical invariant: the rate at which agency accumulates against the rate at which the capacity to answer it does. Technical modernization without matching correction capacity adds to the debt, and it changes the institution's politics without a single decision. The corrective debt calculator is its instrument.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: Action capacity and corrective capacity are tracked on separate axes and compared.
A scope expansion rechecks correction capacity rather than assuming it.
The debt is reported as a number the institution owns, not a one-time audit finding.
entries.genealogy: Names the accumulation Law IV and the invariant describe, so it can be measured rather than only felt.

entries.title: Abstention
entries.bodyHtml:
A system or institution declining to act, treated as a capability rather than a failure to answer. It takes one of three forms. Epistemic abstention says the evidence does not support acting on this case and hands it to someone who might know. Jurisdictional abstention says this is not mine to decide and hands it to the party with standing. Remedial abstention says even if I am probably right, acting now would create a harm that cannot safely be corrected later, and declines until reversal is possible.

It matters because each form is testable and each has a distinct failure mode when absent: epistemic abstention degrades into confident guessing, jurisdictional abstention into scope creep, and remedial abstention into irreversibility. A deployment that cannot abstain in all three forms has no boundary on what it will do with its capability, and exception absorption is what fills the gap.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: The system can decline an action because its evidence is insufficient, and route the case rather than guess.
The system can decline because the question belongs to a different decision-maker, and record the referral.
The system can decline because reversal would be impossible, and state what would make it possible.
entries.genealogy: Names the three refusals the non-conversion principle and the failure-path work imply as capabilities rather than gaps.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A refusal taxonomy in the decision record: declined cases carry which abstention applied and why.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A declined consequential action routed to a named alternative decision-maker.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of declined decisions that record an abstention form, versus silent low-confidence output.

entries.title: Constitutional debt
entries.bodyHtml:
The accumulated divergence between what a system can technically do and what any recorded justification permits it to do. Each widening that occurs as a capability becoming reachable rather than a decision being taken adds to the debt; the automation ratchet is its engine and authority drift is its balance.

It matters because the debt is invisible while it accrues: the system performs well, the grants sit quiet, and the gap grows without a policy document changing. It is the sibling of corrective debt, which measures the gap against the capacity to hear; constitutional debt measures it against the capacity to justify. Both are payable only through the machinery Laws I, II, and XI bind: recorded transitions with stated bases.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: The gap between the capability catalog and the authority surface is measured and reported.
Every widening appears as a recorded transition with a basis, or is reported as debt.
Renewal reviews compare current scope against the original justification, not against last year's scope.
entries.genealogy: Names the accumulation the automation ratchet and silent authority drift produce, parallel to corrective debt.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A reconciliation of the capability catalog against the authority surface, with the ungrantable remainder listed.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An expansion refused, or granted as an explicit transition, because the justification covered less than the new scope.
minimumEvidence.metric: Capability classes exercised in production with no recorded authorization transition.

entries.title: Refusability
entries.bodyHtml:
A system’s ability to let people say “no” without punishment or degradation — including refusing data extraction, risky defaults, or coercive workflows — while still preserving basic access and dignity. Refusability is not “opt-out exists”; it is whether refusal is treated as a legitimate state rather than an error condition.

It is the capability that operationalizes human refusal tolerance, is bounded by the refusal budget, and is protected by the right of exit.
entries.scope: C. Ethotechnic capabilities (what systems must be able to do). What a system must be able to do while it holds consequential authority: halt, reverse, answer a challenge, and learn from the correction.
operationalTests: A refusal produces a non-punitive state change rather than an error or a penalty.
Refusing one workflow does not degrade access to unrelated services.
entries.genealogy: Promotes “no” from an inconvenience to a first-class capability requirement.

categories.heading: D. System states & architectures
categories.descriptionHtml: Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Fail-safe mode
entries.bodyHtml:
The system defaults to the safest possible behavior when uncertain, putting the ability to stop ahead of throughput. In Ethotechnic practice, fail-safe mode is not a generic error page: it is a predesigned degraded state with bounded actions, clear status signals, and immediate escalation paths.

A fail-safe posture should preserve contestability and reduce irreversible harm while operators diagnose the incident.
examples: A medication-order service blocks new high-risk orders during model drift and routes clinicians to manual review with visible restore timing.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Fail-open mode
entries.bodyHtml:
The system defaults to permissiveness under failure — sometimes necessary for continuity, sometimes dangerous. A fail-open mode should be limited in time and come with friction that slows fast automated steps, monitoring, and rapid escalation.

Ethotechnic fail-open design requires explicit thresholds for returning to fail-safe mode when risk rises.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: Fail-open modes have explicit thresholds where they automatically switch to fail-safe or escalate to human review.
examples: A payments API temporarily accepts transactions during dependency outages but caps transfer size and triggers mandatory post-reconciliation review.

entries.title: Fail-silent mode
entries.bodyHtml: A harmful state where a system fails without signaling it. It is the hardest failure to catch, because it hides the lag between harm and response: harm accrues while every indicator reads normal.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Moral crumple zone
entries.bodyHtml:
The person in an automated system who absorbs the blame and the cost when the system fails. Madeleine Clare Elish named the pattern the moral crumple zone in “Moral Crumple Zones” (Engaging Science, Technology, and Society, 2019). In a car, the crumple zone absorbs the force of a crash so the passengers survive. In an automated system, the nearest human absorbs responsibility for the failure, and the system's reputation survives.

Ethotechnics standards are written to move that impact back onto the system and the institution that runs it. The Crumple Zone publishes case analyses of these failures.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Harm visibility
entries.bodyHtml: How plainly a system exposes the human impact of its decisions in real time. High harm visibility combines logs, people's accounts, and alerts, so outside oversight sees past dashboards and automatic halts fire on effects on people as well as on technical anomalies.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Dead zones / moral dead zones
entries.bodyHtml: Places in a system where harm occurs but no one can see, trace, or intervene. Closing dead zones is a goal of oversight horizons.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Escalation horizon
entries.bodyHtml: The predefined point where automated control must yield to human judgment because risk, ambiguity, or the lag between harm and response is rising. At that point the system halts automatically and routes the case to an accountable person before it crosses a threshold it cannot undo.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Interaction surface
entries.bodyHtml: The moments, interfaces, and channels where people experience system decisions and can intervene. Mapping it shows where to add confirmation steps that protect people, where people need more room to act, and where people cannot contest, appeal, or exit.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Maintenance window
entries.bodyHtml:
A scheduled calm state where teams intentionally slow or stop throughput so inspections, upgrades, and rehearsals can happen without crisis pressure. Maintenance windows make stoppability routine instead of reactive.

Each window is negotiated with the people impacted, includes published service guarantees, and documents which safeguards were tested so unfinished work rolls into the shared repair log.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Care retrospective
entries.bodyHtml:
A facilitated reflection held while the system is still in a warning band to examine how maintenance load, emotional labor, and unresolved incidents are accumulating. Care retrospectives combine telemetry with frontline testimony.

They redistribute responsibilities before burnout or harm escalates, triggering new maintenance windows or policy fixes when the team cannot keep absorbing risk.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Repair log
entries.bodyHtml:
A living record of every mitigation, decision, and resource commitment made after a fault. Repair logs make accountability legible by linking who was harmed, who intervened, and what evidence was used. Repair logs include whether affected people were restored, how long it took, and what remains unrepaired.

They inform future care retrospectives, power audits, and service-level reports so follow-up work is traceable and burden does not drift back to the same communities.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.

entries.title: Restoration completeness
entries.bodyHtml: “Restored” means the person is back to the prior state in every downstream system, not only unblocked in the one that erred. Restoration completeness ensures time-to-restore includes reconciliation with dependencies.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: Reconciliation across dependencies confirms restoration beyond the local system.
Affected people confirm their state is restored and downstream impacts are cleared.

entries.title: Downstream harm trace
entries.bodyHtml: A record of where a harmful decision propagated across vendors, data brokers, internal teams, and agencies. Downstream harm traces extend the repair log so remedies follow the harm.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: Every critical action produces a propagation map of downstream recipients.
Trace data is stored with the repair log and accessible during remediation.

entries.title: Shadow queue
entries.bodyHtml: A queue users cannot see — internal backlogs, vendor queues, or “pending review” pools — that still determines outcomes. Shadow queues erode time transparency and contestability.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: Every queue has public existence, time transparency, and bounded duration.
Users can see the queues influencing their case and their place within them.

entries.title: Grant state
entries.bodyHtml:
The current status of a system's recorded permission to act, drawn from a closed set: allowed, review_required, suspended, or revoked. Every action is checked against the state in force at the time it is taken, and every transition is recorded with its cause.

It matters because states are what triggers can move. Without an explicit grant state there is nothing for a review trigger to change, and monitoring stays decorative rather than governing.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: The set of legal states and the legal transitions between them are declared, not implied.
Every transition record names the trigger, the actor, and the timestamp.
Replaying the state history reproduces the authorization status at any past moment.
entries.genealogy: Gives Law VIII an object: an observation is governing only if it can move a grant from one declared state to another.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A state machine definition for grants, with legal transitions and their triggers.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A grant moving to review_required automatically when a dependency lapses.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of state transitions with a recorded cause, and median dwell time in review_required.

entries.title: Capability catalog
entries.bodyHtml:
The record of what a decision system can do, maintained separately from what it is permitted to do. Each entry names an action class, how it was verified, and when the verification was last refreshed, and entries arrive through capability discovery.

It matters because the catalog is what an authority grant is written against. Comparing catalog to grants is the direct test of whether capability has outrun authority, and a catalog nobody refreshes silently stops being that test. A stale entry also removes the ground a revisable delegation stands on, because the grant then rests on a capability nobody has re-verified.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: Every catalog entry carries a verification method and a verification date.
The catalog is diffed against the grant register on a stated cadence.
Capabilities present in the catalog but absent from any grant are listed, not hidden.
entries.genealogy: The counterpart object to the grant register: one records what is possible, the other what is permitted, and the gap between them is the governable quantity.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A capability catalog with action class, verification method, and last-verified date.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A stale catalog entry blocking a grant renewal until re-verified.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of catalog entries verified within their declared refresh interval.

entries.title: Dependency state
entries.bodyHtml:
The current degree to which an institution relies on a system: who depends on it, what would break without it, what expertise has been retained, and how long substitution would take. This is institutional dependence, meaning what the institution has come to rely on, and it is distinct from the record-level dependence in STD-07 Article III, which asks what a particular record rests on.

It matters because dependence quietly removes corrections from the menu. Tracked as a state, it can be scored through exposure score, read against the deployment's substrate profile, and countered by replenishing institutional reversibility. A dependence that also supplies the deployment's own evaluation is worse than its score suggests, which is why the record carries evaluation independence.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: A dependency record lists dependents, retained expertise, alternatives, and substitution time.
The record is refreshed on a cadence rather than at incident time.
A rise in dependence without a matching correction investment appears in a governance review.
entries.genealogy: Gives Law V an object and distinguishes institutional dependence from the record dependence already governed by STD-07 Article III.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A dependency record for the deployment, with dependents, alternatives, and retained expertise.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A dependency review that changed a roadmap decision, recorded with its reasoning.
minimumEvidence.metric: Number of dependent workflows and days to substitution, tracked quarterly.

entries.title: Substrate profile
entries.bodyHtml:
A classification of a model deployment by nine properties, used instead of asking only whether the model is open or closed. The properties are weight access, runtime control, update authority, version stability, revocation, substitutability, observability, standing, and dependency. Two deployments of the same model can carry entirely different profiles.

It matters because the governance burden follows the profile rather than the license. The profile says which properties the institution holds itself and which it has left with a provider, which is what determines its real institutional reversibility and its dependency state.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: All nine properties are recorded per deployment, not per model.
A property held by a provider is named as such, with the contractual basis for relying on it.
The profile is re-scored when the provider, contract, or hosting arrangement changes.
entries.genealogy: Replaces the open-weights debate with a classification of deployments.

references.label: Open weights and the delegation boundary

minimumEvidence.artifact: A substrate profile record scoring all nine properties for the deployment.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A procurement decision changed after the profile revealed no revocation control.
minimumEvidence.metric: Count of the nine properties held by the institution rather than the provider.

entries.title: Bifurcation by contestability
entries.bodyHtml:
Systems split into high-contestability lanes (slower, trusted, deployable in high stakes) and low-contestability lanes (fast, then blocked). The split protects people by matching speed to the reversibility of the decision.

It is the architectural answer to velocity friction: decisions that can be contested may run fast, and decisions that cannot must not.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: A decision’s speed is gated by its reversibility and appeal rights.
Decisions with severe or irreversible consequences are routed to a lane with binding review before harm propagates.
entries.genealogy: Turns contestability into a routing rule rather than an after-the-fact remedy.

entries.title: Typed decision model
entries.bodyHtml:
A model that takes a block of state and a set of questions with fixed answers, and returns a chosen value with a probability distribution and a confidence margin instead of text. It gives no reasons. Typical uses are routing, triage, tool gating, and approval checks.

It matters because a cheap judgment gets placed at every branch, and authority follows it into places that do not look like decisions: the decision threshold that turns a score into an action, the shaping hop that decides what the decider sees, and the reasons nobody produced. The method governs it like any other delegate. The explainer names the six places its authority sits, and the decision record carries a typed_judgment block for what it decided.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
operationalTests: Every consequential decision a typed decision model contributes to has a decision record with a typed_judgment block naming the pinned model version.
The threshold that acts on the model's output is a policy record, not a configuration value.
Confidence is recorded with its semantics, and a margin is not reported as a probability of being right.
entries.genealogy: A new substrate that tests the method's substrate independence: the unit of governance is the consequential decision, whatever component made it.

references.label: Typed decision models and where their authority lives

minimumEvidence.artifact: Decision records with a typed_judgment block: pinned decider, question schema hash, distribution, confidence semantics, threshold policy, and reason provenance.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A model upgrade suspending the thresholds tuned against the previous version until they are re-set.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of decisions involving a typed decision model whose record names a pinned model version and a threshold policy.

entries.title: Rescue register
entries.bodyHtml:
A record of failures that occurred and were caught by a person before they reached anyone else. Each entry carries the near-miss condition, the person who caught it, the labor spent catching it, and whether the source condition was later fixed.

An incident count that omits these rescues reports the number of times the institution was not lucky. It is the recording half of compensated performance: where that term names the condition, this names the ledger.

STD-06 §3.3 requires it as a safety-case artifact, and non-expropriation of resilience is why the entry has to carry the labor. A rescue costs the person who performs it, and an institution that reads the same rescue as evidence of a safe system has booked their compensation as its own performance.

A rescue that repeats against the same unfixed condition is the strongest signal the register holds. It is evidence about the condition rather than about the competence of whoever keeps catching it.
entries.scope: D. System states & architectures. Operating postures, records, and architectures that decide whether an error is contained, recorded, or amplified.
examples: A reconciliation defect produces no incidents for a year because nurses catch every mismatch before dispensing. The register shows 300 rescues against one unfixed interface and 4,000 hours of checking nobody rostered.

categories.heading: E. Human limits & experience
categories.descriptionHtml: The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Finitude
entries.bodyHtml:
The bodily, cognitive, emotional, and temporal limits all humans share. Ethotechnics treats finitude as a design input, not an inconvenience or a staffing problem to be hidden.

Systems that ignore finitude convert predictable limits into preventable harm, usually through alert overload, impossible response clocks, or unpaid maintenance expectations.
examples: An incident-response rotation caps overnight escalations and enforces recovery windows so operators can keep working safely through prolonged outages.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Cognitive saturation point
entries.bodyHtml: The load level at which human decision quality collapses — too many alerts, too little time, or excessive context switching. Design lowers it by slowing fast automated steps, simplifying the screens and channels where people act, and staffing to the real volume of upkeep.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Compassion bandwidth
entries.bodyHtml: The sustainable amount of emotional labor a system asks of people — care teams, moderators, frontline staff, or users. When a system asks for more, people start avoiding tasks the system punishes, and the system runs on their burnout.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Administrative shame
entries.bodyHtml: The feeling of being personally at fault for harms produced by system design. Often a signal that moral overhead is too high.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Virtue as access control
entries.bodyHtml:
Composure, clarity, gratitude, “professionalism,” or patience become requirements for baseline safety or remedy.

Virtue as access control turns emotional labor into a gate and magnifies administrative shame. Violates affect-invariance.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Affect-invariance
entries.bodyHtml:
Baseline safety and remedy should not change based on distress, fatigue, disability, fear, or anger. Primary threat model: virtue as access control.

Affect-invariance reinforces care floor guarantees and protects contestability.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Dread work
entries.bodyHtml: Tasks people avoid because the system punishes mistakes or withholds relief. It is a sign that the system has no cushioning at its boundaries, that its decisions are hard to challenge, and that people's capacity for emotional labor is running out.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Refusal budget
entries.bodyHtml: The number of times a person can decline, pause, or question a request without retaliation. A refusal budget backed by refusal tolerance and rights of exit prevents coercion, and heat maps of refusal show where budgets are running out.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Behavioral shaping
entries.bodyHtml: The way systems nudge, constrain, or normalize user behavior through defaults and design choices. Velocity friction and narrow limits on what people may do amplify it, because each is itself a way of shaping behavior.
examples: Default opt-ins normalize data sharing even when users are uncertain.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.

entries.title: Error-bearing party
entries.bodyHtml:
Anyone who absorbs the consequences of a system's errors: the people its decisions fall on, and the staff whose corrective labor the system depends on to stay usable. They are usually the first to see failures and the last able to act on them.

It matters because exposure without a route into the system is wasted signal. Identifying error-bearing parties is the precondition for corrective standing, and failing to identify them is how heroism-dependent systems keep looking reliable.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.
operationalTests: The standing register names error-bearing parties by role, including internal operators.
Exception-handling labor is counted and attributed rather than absorbed silently.
Parties named in the register can be reached by the system's own channels, not only by escalation.
entries.genealogy: Names the class Law VII grants standing to, and deliberately includes the operators whose corrective labor the system consumes.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A standing register listing error-bearing parties per decision class.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An operator raising a challenge through the same mechanism available to affected people.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of decision classes with at least one named error-bearing party.

entries.title: Adaptive capacity
entries.bodyHtml:
The finite human resource an arrangement consumes when it demands that people adapt to it: the attention, memory, flexibility, time, health, and care that keep a mismatched system functional. It is finite and politically consequential: the resource ethotechnical design exists to spend only when necessary, and to preserve when an arrangement could instead absorb the complexity itself.

It matters because an arrangement that treats adaptive capacity as unlimited reads the people who compensate for it as resilient rather than as a resource being consumed. The discipline's working distinction is between compensatory adaptation, which is effort required because the arrangement failed to accommodate foreseeable reality, and the productive or reciprocal adaptation that learning, cooperation, and care require.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.
operationalTests: Each consequential workflow names the adaptive capacity it requires of its users, not only of its operators.
Demands that foreseeable variation could remove are treated as design gaps rather than as user burdens.
The measure distinguishes capacity consumed by mismatch from capacity spent by choice.
entries.genealogy: The design-side reading of Axiom 1 (Finitude): what an arrangement must spend, and who must spend it.

entries.title: Executive function (as a class axis)
entries.bodyHtml:
The idea that modern systems sort people by their capacity for sustained administrative work: tracking tasks, managing documents, and navigating ambiguity. The sorting turns disability and burnout into structural disadvantage.

It connects cognitive saturation and dread work to the stratification produced by administrative shame.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.
operationalTests: Administrative load is treated as an axis of exclusion, not a personal failing.
Interfaces offer low-executive-function paths (single actions, clear clocks) as defaults.
entries.genealogy: Reads executive-function demand as a class mechanism, extending the burden vocabulary.

entries.title: Human factors
entries.bodyHtml:
A discipline that studies how systems interact with real human limits — fatigue, confusion, stress — often revealing that “user error” is design failure.

It is the empirical home of cognitive saturation and finitude, and the reason operator-centered design treats frontline workers as safety components.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.
operationalTests: An error is attributed to design before it is attributed to the user.
Human limits are measured and feed back into interface and workflow design.
entries.genealogy: Imports the established field that grounds the human-limits category in practice.

entries.title: Operator-centered
entries.bodyHtml:
Design that treats frontline workers as safety components and ensures they have authority, tools, and non-punitive reporting to prevent harm. It rejects heroism-dependent systems, which offload safety onto individual endurance.

Operator-centered systems extend the same refusal tolerance to workers that they extend to users.
entries.scope: E. Human limits & experience. The limits of human time, attention, and endurance that a system's clocks, review loads, and correction paths must fit within.
operationalTests: Frontline workers hold authority to pause or escalate, in addition to reporting.
Reporting harm is non-punitive and loops back into design change.
entries.genealogy: Applies the capability requirements to the people who operate the system, not only its users.

categories.heading: F. Burden & load
categories.descriptionHtml: Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Burden distribution
entries.bodyHtml:
How a system allocates the cost of operation or failure — time, attention, stress, and emotional labor — across users, staff, and institutions. Burden distribution determines who keeps the service running when conditions degrade.

Measuring it means recording each transfer, then redesigning flows so the hidden labor shrinks instead of becoming normal.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
examples: A support process shifts repetitive evidence collection from users to internal case assembly, reducing repeat submissions.

entries.title: Burden gradient
entries.bodyHtml:
The slope of effort and risk across roles or communities. A steep burden gradient means those with the least power carry the heaviest operational load while decision-makers feel little friction.

Mapping the gradient exposes where to redistribute work through fair burden distribution and reduce moral overhead.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Failure load
entries.bodyHtml: The amount of harm generated when the system fails, and how many people it reaches. The aim is an architecture whose failures stay small, supported by graceful degradation.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Burden transfer event
entries.bodyHtml:
A moment when system failure pushes labor, risk, or emotional work onto people, often leaving them extra work to do the right thing. Burden transfer events are observable handoffs: the system stops carrying what it promised to carry.

Common signals include repeated documentation requests, forced channel switching, and manual triage queues that appear without new staffing.
examples: After an identity-verification outage, users are told to restart the process across three channels and re-upload evidence already submitted.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Maintenance metabolism
entries.bodyHtml:
The baseline flow of upkeep — patching, cleaning, rehearsing, and caring — that keeps a service alive when nothing is on fire. Healthy maintenance metabolism is budgeted, scheduled, and shared rather than squeezed between crises.

Falling below it signals rising maintenance debt and invites maintenance windows before fragility compounds.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Maintenance debt
entries.bodyHtml:
Accumulated obligations from skipping basic upkeep. The interest is paid in slower recovery, brittle systems, and people burning out to keep things running.

Paying it down requires restoring the maintenance metabolism, scheduling maintenance windows, and tracking work in the repair log.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Moral overhead
entries.bodyHtml:
Extra work users or operators must do to behave ethically within a poorly designed system. Moral overhead appears when the default workflow produces harm unless people add compensating care, vigilance, or documentation.

Ethotechnic design aims to move this overhead back into the system through clearer defaults, better safeguards, and funded maintenance capacity.
examples: Moderators manually reverse ranking decisions every day because harmful content controls are too weak at launch.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Temporal exaction
entries.bodyHtml:
Uncompensated seizure of life-hours (time, attention, opportunity cost) as the price of accessing a right or correction.

Temporal exaction is a form of extraction that inflates the user burden ratio.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Asymmetric sustaining
entries.bodyHtml:
When one group continually absorbs the toil of keeping a system alive so another group can move fast or claim success. It often hides behind gratitude for “resilience” while masking extraction.

Ethotechnic practice flattens this by lowering the burden gradient and designing for stoppability so resilience is institutional, not personal.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Fragility subsidy
entries.bodyHtml: The unpaid labor, vigilance, or emotional buffering people contribute to keep brittle systems functioning. Fragility subsidies hide what a system costs to run, inflate success metrics, and deepen asymmetric sustaining.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Degradation/restoration asymmetry
entries.bodyHtml:
It is cheap or fast to harm or change someone’s state, but slow and costly to reverse.

Degradation/restoration asymmetry inflates time-to-restore and compounds moral debt.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Endurance-as-allocation
entries.bodyHtml:
Who gets the right outcome is determined by who can survive the correction path, not by who is substantively right.

Endurance-as-allocation weaponizes endurance asymmetry and steepens the burden gradient.
