entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Stamina pricing
entries.bodyHtml:
Rights exist in theory, but the option to claim them is priced in paperwork, waiting, and persistence.

Stamina pricing shows up in punitive friction and drives attrition-as-resolution.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Burden index
entries.bodyHtml:
A burden index counts the time and effort a system demands of people who comply with it, appeal against it, or recover from it.

It counts the minutes, retries, and documents each journey takes. Published on a schedule, it shows whether the cost to people rose or fell since the last report.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Harm internalization
entries.bodyHtml: Designing systems so creators and operators bear the costs of failures instead of externalizing them to users or society. It keeps failures from falling hardest on the most vulnerable and stops costs being pushed onto others.
examples: A vendor funds remediation and user support when its model causes harm.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Maintenance ethics
entries.bodyHtml: The position that responsibility for a system continues after deployment, through monitoring, updates, incident response, and repair. It treats routine upkeep and the record of repairs as commitments that do not end.
examples: Teams publish repair logs and schedule maintenance windows after each major release.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.

entries.title: Channel switching penalty
entries.bodyHtml: The hidden harm of being bounced between phone, email, chat, and portal channels, often resetting clocks or losing context. Channel switching penalties increase procedural burden and delay repair.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: Switching channels does not reset case age or evidence sets.
Case history and documentation follow the claimant across every channel.

entries.title: Evidence burden ceiling
entries.bodyHtml:
A hard cap on documentation demands placed on claimants for a given harm class. Evidence burden ceilings enforce fair burden distribution during appeals.

Feeds into: user burden ratio, burden index.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: Maximum documentation counts, minutes, or steps are enforced in UI and policy.
Requests beyond the ceiling require justification and escalation approval.

entries.title: Burden ceiling
entries.bodyHtml: A limit on the procedural work a system may demand of a person seeking safety, correction, or relief. It is set for each kind of harm and enforced through the interface, staffing, and policy. It caps the work a person must do to correct the system's errors, and crossing it moves the effort onto the institution under the burden inversion rule.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: A ceiling exists per workflow (for example, appeal submission must take ≤10 minutes, ≤5 steps, ≤2 documents).
The user burden ratio is tracked and stays below the ceiling.
When the ceiling is exceeded, the system shifts to burden inversion, doing the work first, or offers a staffed alternative.

entries.title: Evidence recycling
entries.bodyHtml: The system reuses previously verified information so people do not have to re-prove identity or harm repeatedly. Evidence recycling applies continuity of state to documentation as well as to case status.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: Previously verified identity or harm evidence auto-attaches to new cases.
Continuity of state is applied to evidence across workflows and channels.

entries.title: Verification harm
entries.bodyHtml:
When verification itself causes harm through delays, denials, exclusion, or stress spirals. It adds to the time and effort the system demands of people, and when people cannot realistically comply, it can leave them unable to challenge the decision.

Reducing verification harm means eliminating redundant proofs, honoring prior evidence, and shortening time-to-resolution for urgent needs.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: Utility expiry attributable to verification steps is measured and tracked.
Verification workflows are revised when measured harm exceeds agreed thresholds.
examples: A family loses temporary housing eligibility because identity checks require documents already submitted in a previously approved case.

entries.title: Residual complexity
entries.bodyHtml:
The friction, ambiguity, and repair labor that remains unresolved after a formal model simplifies a workflow. A formal system does not eliminate what it cannot represent; it redistributes the burden of dealing with it. What is left out of the formal representation becomes residual complexity.

The political question is who has to carry this residual, and with what power to contest or correct the system. Where a system has no repair channel, users bend around rigid software, workers patch edge cases by hand, and citizens spend their own time on bureaucratic procedure.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: The volume and duration of manual interventions needed to make automated outputs usable are tracked.
The residual effort of resolving model failures is compensated, and a contestability mechanism exists that can change the outcome.
entries.genealogy: States the sequence the method starts from: formal simplification leaves residual complexity, someone has to carry it, and who carries it is a political question.

entries.title: Compensatory adaptation
entries.bodyHtml:
Human effort required mainly because an arrangement failed to accommodate foreseeable reality. Examples are remembering passwords, coordinating fragmented services, reproducing information the institution already holds, repairing software, and requesting the same exception again and again. It is distinct from the productive or reciprocal adaptation that learning, cooperation, compromise, and care require.

It matters because adaptive capacity is finite, and compensatory adaptation spends it without returning anything to the person who spent it. Where it accumulates, the arrangement remains stable precisely because people bend around it, which is why ethotechnical design treats recurring compensatory effort as a design failure to be eliminated or absorbed upstream rather than as user resilience.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: For each recurring user or operator demand, the design names whether the arrangement could absorb it instead.
Compensatory effort is counted in burden accounting, not read as user capability.
Repeated instances of the same exception raise the rule for review rather than the efficiency of the exception process.
entries.genealogy: The burden-side counterpart of adaptive capacity: what the discipline exists to minimize, and the falsified denominator's human face.

entries.title: Compensatory inputs
entries.bodyHtml: Eight kinds of uncounted work that keep an institution running. They are usually read as personal dedication or routine operation. The eight are repair (fixing defects), coordination (bridging silos), interpretation (deciphering rules), anticipation (predicting failures), affective work (absorbing friction), self-regulation (setting aside bodily or schedule needs), risk-bearing (absorbing liability), and temporal work (waiting, chasing, and rearranging schedules).
examples: A patient spends sixteen hours coordinating records across four clinics, serving as uncredited coordination infrastructure for an interoperability failure.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: Time in frontline roles is broken down by the eight categories, and non-formal repair is reported beside formal tasks.
Each compensatory input is linked to the upstream fix, in data integration or policy, that would remove it.
entries.genealogy: Draws on feminist social reproduction theory and resilience engineering, and turns them into categories an auditor can count.

references.label: The human subsidy to institutional continuity

entries.title: Cost assignment / burden shifting
entries.bodyHtml:
A mechanism where systems offload the labor of safety, clarity, and follow-through onto individuals (forms, documentation, vigilance) while keeping institutional obligation low. It is how “choice” becomes unpaid work.

Cost assignment is the engine of burden transfer events and the inverse of fair burden distribution.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: The party that benefits from a decision is measured against the party that bears its cost.
A safety obligation is not satisfied by moving paperwork to the affected individual.
entries.genealogy: Names the transfer by which institutions externalize the cost of their own operation.

entries.title: Attention tax
entries.bodyHtml:
The ongoing monitoring burden imposed on individuals to prevent harm: checking portals, tracking deadlines, resubmitting documents, watching for silent rule changes. Attention becomes a cost of staying eligible.

It is the lived form of the burden index and a steady drain that temporal exaction measures over time.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: Monitoring cost is quantified and attributed to a design decision.
Silent rule changes that require vigilance are treated as a burden defect.
entries.genealogy: Converts vigilance into a measurable tax paid in attention.

entries.title: Audit burden ceiling
entries.bodyHtml:
A hard cap on the human labor a person spends producing evidence for an institution's own audit. An evidence burden ceiling bounds the labor of proving a claim against a decision; this bounds the labor of describing a system to the party that already owns its records.

Feeds into: user burden ratio, exhaustion-biased instrument.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: one review cycle. Target / floor / ceiling: target 20 minutes or less of respondent labor per instrument; floor 30 minutes; ceiling 60 minutes. Breach action: the instrument returns not established rather than a score, and the operator's own records answer the question instead. A respondent who cannot answer inside the ceiling has not failed the audit.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
operationalTests: Each instrument states the respondent labor it will consume before the respondent begins.
Where records the operator already holds can answer the question, the respondent is not asked.
A non-response is recorded as a gap in the instrument, not as a passing result.

entries.title: Verification tax
entries.bodyHtml:
The cost of establishing whether a machine-generated claim is true, paid by the person the claim was generated for. Generation takes seconds. Verification of plausible prose against its sources takes minutes of high-load scanning — and the sources are frequently the scans, faxes, and unindexed records the system summarized in the first place. A fluent draft that cannot show where it got each claim does not save time; it moves the time onto the reader and hides it inside a metric that only counts generation.

It is the burden-side twin of compensated performance. That term covers labor spent making a system's errors invisible. This one covers labor spent making its outputs usable — and a system can be well built, fast, and accurate, and still tax its readers, because the tax is levied per claim and no metric counts it.

It differs from verification harm, which is the burden of proving eligibility to an institution. This is the burden of trusting a machine's summary of a record the reader cannot cheaply check. And it differs from audit burden ceiling, which caps the labor a respondent spends producing evidence. Here the reader did not choose to verify; the output was presented as if the work were done.

The checkable form is claim-level anchoring: every displayed claim links to its source on demand, and a claim the system cannot anchor is suppressed rather than shown. The explainability evals test it.
entries.scope: F. Burden & load. Who carries the time, cost, and risk when a system runs or fails, and whether that transfer is recorded.
examples: An AI summary states a documented penicillin allergy. Confirming it against twelve unindexed outside-hospital scans takes eight minutes; the generation took four seconds and is what the metric counted.

categories.heading: G. Measures & indicators
categories.descriptionHtml: Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Composed latency
entries.bodyHtml:
The time a chain of delegations takes, measured from decision records rather than nominal per-hop promises. Hops that run in series compose additively, and the time a human has to act is the intervention window minus the latency the upstream hops have already consumed.

Composed latency shows how a human in the loop can be a fiction: each hop can promise a fast review while the composition consumes the window a person would have needed. A chain whose composed latency leaves no measured human window cannot run unattended.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Hop latencies are measured from decision records on a declared cadence.
The composed window is recomputed whenever any hop's measured latency changes materially.
A chain leaving no measured human window does not run unattended.
entries.genealogy: STD-09 Part B binds composed latency because per-hop clocks can each look compliant while the composition owes no one any time.

minimumEvidence.artifact: Composed-window measurements with the hop latencies they were computed from.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A chain whose window closes is moved to confirm mode or narrowed, visibly, on the record.
minimumEvidence.metric: Composed window in ms per chain decision, trended against the intervention budget.

entries.title: Silent-harm discovery
entries.bodyHtml:
The deployer-side duty to find harm nobody complained about: error, reversal, and remedy rates computed per affected population from records the operator already retains, on a declared cadence. Standing gives the party who challenges a route into the system; it does nothing for the party who never challenges.

A deployment whose only harm signal is an incoming claim is blind by construction to the populations least able to file one. STD-06 §2.4 treats a materially worse rate for any population as a threshold breach, so divergence is found by measurement or it is a violation.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Error, reversal, and remedy rates are computed per affected population, not only in aggregate.
A materially worse rate for any population triggers the declared breach action.
The operator can name a harm its measurement found before any affected party reported it.
entries.genealogy: STD-06 §2.4 added discovery without a claim because extraction by endurance hides harm from the dashboard precisely where complaint is least likely.

minimumEvidence.artifact: Per-population rate series with the cadence and the records they were computed from.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A materially worse rate for any population is treated as a threshold breach, not as context.
minimumEvidence.metric: Rate divergence per population per period, against the declared threshold.

entries.title: Moral performance indicators (MPIs)
entries.bodyHtml: Moral performance indicators (MPIs) is an older name for the five measures on the measurement tiers page. The site now calls them measures. They are rule change after upheld challenges, appeal success rate, burden ratio, reversibility rate, and time-to-halt (TTH). Each shows whether a system can still be stopped, reversed, and challenged, or what its errors cost the people who carry them. They sit beside KPIs: KPIs track how fast a system grows, and these measures track how safely and fairly it operates.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Service-level indicators of justice (SLJs)
entries.bodyHtml:
Operational metrics tied directly to fairness, safety, and dignity. Service-level indicators of justice (SLJs) sit alongside uptime and latency, so fairness, safety, and dignity are managed as production requirements.

SLJs include reversal timeliness, appeal passage rate, and burden exposure by cohort — each with escalation thresholds and owners.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
examples: A municipality tracks median time-to-restore benefits after wrongful denial and triggers mandatory review when thresholds are exceeded.

entries.title: Institutional metabolism mapping
entries.bodyHtml:
A diagnostic map of where labor, emotional labor, time, and money go inside an institution. It shows the routine upkeep, who carries the heaviest load, and where value is taken without return.

Teams use the map to set fairness and safety measures, redesign roles, and decide where to invest new maintenance windows.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Time-to-halt (TTH)
entries.bodyHtml:
Seconds between a harmful process beginning and the system stopping it. It is the measured side of stoppability.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly p95; monthly p99. Target / floor / ceiling: target ≤ 30s (automated) / ≤ 5 min (human), floor 15 min, ceiling 60 min. Owner: traceable ownership (required). Breach action: trigger ethical circuit breakers, safe pause, or rollback lane activation with escalation. Public surface: receipt + time transparency showing halt status and decision artifact.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Time-to-restore (TTR)
entries.bodyHtml:
How long it takes to reverse harm and return a person to their prior state. Low TTR is a signal of reversibility.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly p95; monthly median. Target / floor / ceiling: target ≤ 24h, floor ≤ 72h, ceiling 7d. Owner: traceable ownership (required). Breach action: activate rollback lanes, switch to staffed remediation, or trigger safe pause with escalation. Public surface: receipt + time transparency with restoration ETA and decision artifact.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Appeal passage rate
entries.bodyHtml:
The share of appeals resolved in favor of the person who appealed. A low rate can mean appeals are not being heard. A high rate means many decisions were wrong, which is evidence against the rule that produced them, and the count goes to that rule's owner. Either way, it is an early sign of whether contestability works in practice.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly rolling median; monthly review. Target / floor / ceiling: target 10–20% by harm class, floor 5%, ceiling 30% (investigate systemic error). Owner: traceable ownership (required). Breach action: trigger decision-rule audits, staffing surges, or pause automation in the affected class. Public surface: published appeal outcomes with receipt, time transparency, and decision artifacts.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Irreversibility index
entries.bodyHtml:
The share of system actions that cannot be undone. Aim to keep this as low as possible through reversibility and graceful degradation.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly p95; monthly median. Target / floor / ceiling: target ≤ 1%, floor ≤ 2%, ceiling 5%. Owner: traceable ownership (required). Breach action: invoke ethical circuit breakers, activate rollback lanes, or trigger safe pause. Public surface: receipts and time transparency on irreversible boundaries.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Irreversibility budget
entries.bodyHtml: A predefined cap on the share of actions allowed to be effectively irreversible in a given system or workflow class. Budgets force designers to minimize irreversible boundaries and build rollback lanes for everything else.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: A documented budget exists per critical-action class (for example, account closures or benefit terminations).
The irreversibility index is measured continuously and compared with the budget.
A budget breach trips an ethical circuit breaker (pause, rollback, or escalation), not a retrospective.

entries.title: User burden ratio
entries.bodyHtml:
How much work a user must perform to correct or navigate system errors. This metric feeds directly into fair burden distribution.

Interpretation: UBR must be evaluated against the evidence burden ceiling (documentation) plus time/steps caps (process).

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly median; monthly p95. Target / floor / ceiling: target ≤ 10 minutes, ≤ 5 steps, ≤ 2 documents; floor ≤ 15 minutes, ≤ 8 steps; ceiling 20 minutes / 10 steps. Owner: traceable ownership (required). Breach action: switch to burden inversion, offer staffed alternatives, or trigger safe pause. Public surface: receipt + time transparency + decision artifact showing burden caps.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Human substitution index
entries.bodyHtml:
A measure of how often humans must step in to compensate for system shortcomings — manual reviews, ad hoc patches, or empathy work. A rising index shows a system that runs on extraordinary effort, and makes the case for investing in controlled ways to degrade.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly median; monthly review. Target / floor / ceiling: target ≤ 5% of cases, floor 10%, ceiling 20%. Owner: traceable ownership (required). Breach action: expand graceful degradation, add staffing, or pause automation in the affected class. Public surface: receipt + time transparency that flags human review and decision artifact.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Moral debt
entries.bodyHtml:
The accumulated harm a system has caused but not repaired. It grows as the lag between harm and response lengthens and people lose trust. It is paid down through tiered remedies, repair records people can read, and a shorter time to restore people.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: monthly backlog review; quarterly audit. Target / floor / ceiling: target 0 unresolved cases, floor ≤ 30 days outstanding, ceiling 90 days. Owner: traceable ownership (required). Breach action: trigger restitution sprints, funding escalation, or safe pause of new harm classes. Public surface: repair log updates plus receipts and time transparency on restoration timelines.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Signal credibility
entries.bodyHtml:
The trustworthiness of alerts, metrics, and reports used to govern a system.

High signal credibility pairs transparent sampling, explainability for accountability, and human testimony so warnings trigger action instead of alert fatigue or dismissal.

Targets & breach behavior. Measurement window: weekly precision/recall review; monthly audit. Target / floor / ceiling: target ≥ 0.85 precision, floor ≥ 0.70, ceiling false-positive rate ≥ 0.40. Owner: traceable ownership (required). Breach action: pause dependent automation, recalibrate models, or require human confirmation. Public surface: published signal health via receipt, time transparency, and decision artifacts.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.

entries.title: Identity fragility index
entries.bodyHtml:
A measure of how likely identity or eligibility checks are to fail under ordinary life variance such as name changes, relocation, disability, or housing instability. High fragility indicates brittle verification design rather than user fault.

Reducing fragility requires multi-path verification and tolerance for common variation in identity data.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Failure rates for common life events are measured and tracked.
False-negative rates are reported by group and monitored over time.
examples: A service tracks false negatives after surname changes and adjusts matching logic plus manual override policy to prevent exclusion.

entries.title: Consent revocation latency
entries.bodyHtml:
The time from a person saying “I revoke consent” to system behavior changing everywhere it should — across products, processors, and data stores. Low revocation latency keeps consent journeys credible.

Latency targets should be contractual, monitored, and tied to escalation when dependent systems lag.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Time-to-effective-revocation is measured across processors and data stores.
Revocation SLAs trigger alerts when latency exceeds agreed bounds.
examples: A user revokes ad personalization and sees targeting stop across first-party and vendor systems within a documented SLA window.

entries.title: Repair debt interest rate
entries.bodyHtml:
The rate at which unrepaired harm compounds through financial penalties, health risk, displacement risk, or reputational spread. This metric converts moral debt into explicit time-bound obligations.

Higher interest rates prioritize faster interventions and stronger restitution commitments.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Compounding curves are quantified for each harm class with bounded-duration rules.
Remediation plans use the interest rate to prioritize funding and repair timelines.
examples: A case model estimates how each week of unresolved wrongful denial increases downstream housing instability and required compensation.

entries.title: Exposure score
entries.bodyHtml:
A composite indicator of how much risk an institution carries by relying on a system, defined as dependency depth multiplied by substitution cost multiplied by correction latency. Depth is the number of dependents whose criticality is high or critical. Substitution cost is the estimate in the unit the dependency record states, such as person-weeks. Correction latency is in hours from a decision to intervene to the intervention taking effect. The score is read as a trend, and compared across deployments only where substitution cost is stated in the same unit.

It matters because the three factors are usually owned by different teams and never multiplied. A system can look acceptable on each factor alone and still leave the institution unable to act, which is exactly what dependency state tracking exists to surface.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: All three factors are measured from records rather than estimated in a workshop.
The score is recomputed on a fixed cadence and its trend is reported, not only its level.
A rise driven by any single factor triggers the same review as a rise driven by all three.
entries.genealogy: Makes the Law V claim quantitative so that dependence can be compared across deployments and over time.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A scored dependency record showing depth, substitution cost, and correction latency inputs.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A quarterly recomputation whose rise opened a reversibility investment decision.
minimumEvidence.metric: Exposure score per deployment, trended quarter over quarter.
minimumEvidence.definition: Structural risk carried by an institution's reliance on one deployment.
minimumEvidence.unit: high- or critical-criticality dependents × the record's substitution-cost unit × hours
minimumEvidence.dataSource: Dependency record, substitution study, and intervention drill timings.
minimumEvidence.calculation: dependency depth (dependents whose criticality is high or critical) x substitution cost (in the unit the dependency record states) x correction latency (hours).
minimumEvidence.threshold: No absolute target; a rise of more than 25% quarter over quarter opens a review.

entries.title: Substitution cost
entries.bodyHtml:
What it would take to replace a system with an alternative that meets the same obligation. It is counted in staff-weeks of work, retained expertise, contractual exit terms, and the time before the alternative carries production load. Measured, it is a number; assumed, it is a guess.

It matters because substitution cost is the hinge between a working switch and institutional reversibility, and it is the factor that dominates exposure score in mature deployments. A high and unmeasured cost is how a right of exit becomes nominal.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: The estimate is derived from a costed alternative, not from a vendor comparison sheet.
Contractual exit terms and data egress costs are included in the figure.
The estimate is validated at least once against a partial substitution actually performed.
entries.genealogy: Isolates the factor that converts reliability into lock-in, so Law V and Law VI can be assessed separately.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A costed substitution study for the deployment, dated and owned.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A partial substitution performed in a rehearsal, with actuals compared to estimate.
minimumEvidence.metric: Staff-weeks and elapsed days to bring an alternative to production load.
minimumEvidence.dataSource: Substitution study, contract terms, and rehearsal actuals.

entries.title: Evaluation layer
entries.bodyHtml:
The level of the stack at which an evaluation holds: model, agent, delegation, institution, or consequence. Every suite and case carries its layer so a clean result at one level is never read as a result at another.

It matters because assurance overstates itself when a result at one layer is read as a result at another. A model eval says nothing about whether the authority grant is still valid or whether the institution retains the correction capacity to act on what the eval found. A layer also has to be staffed by someone other than the executor, which is what evaluation independence names.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Every eval case declares its layer, and the declaration is enforced by the suite schema.
Reports state the layer alongside the result rather than in an appendix.
A claim about institution-level behavior cites at least one institution-layer case.
entries.genealogy: Implements Law X by making the layer a required field rather than an implicit property of the test harness.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An eval suite schema with a required layer field on every case.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A claim rejected in review for citing a model-layer result as a delegation-layer finding.
minimumEvidence.metric: Distribution of cases across the five layers per suite.

entries.title: Exit cost
entries.bodyHtml:
What it costs the dependent party to stop depending on a system: money, time, records that must be reconstructed, relationships that must be re-established, and access that is lost. Exit cost is measured from the side of the person or organization the system's decisions land on, which distinguishes it from substitution cost, the institution's own cost to replace the system. The two move independently; an institution can be free to replace a system its population cannot afford to leave.

It matters because a party who can leave at acceptable cost bears a system's errors only until they leave. A party who cannot leave bears every error for as long as the system makes it. For that party, the institution's own correction capacity is the only correction there is, and exit cost measures how much depends on it. It also limits what silence can mean: where people cannot leave, a lack of complaints is not evidence of a lack of errors. Exit cost turns a right of exit from a clause into a quantity. It rises by drift, as records accumulate in the system's format and alternatives go unmaintained.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Exit cost is estimated per affected population, not assumed from the existence of an exit clause.
The estimate is revisited at each renewal or expansion of the grant, and a rise is treated as a rise in what the institution owes.
Standing and reversal paths are scaled to measured exit cost rather than to complaint volume.
entries.genealogy: Names the instrument the theory essay on dependence running both ways uses to bound what an institution owes a population that cannot leave its system.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A per-population estimate of exit cost, with the components it was built from.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A correction path widened because the exit cost estimate for its population rose.
minimumEvidence.metric: Exit cost per affected population, tracked across grant renewals.

entries.title: Falsified denominator
entries.bodyHtml:
An accounting distortion in which efficiency, speed, or productivity metrics count only what is spent inside the machine boundary. Human time, attention, and repair work outside it are counted as zero. Leaving that work out of the denominator makes the institution look more efficient than it is.

A system that takes 50 milliseconds of server time but 45 minutes of human troubleshooting across phone trees and appeal queues is not fast; it has falsified its denominator. Refusing the falsified denominator is the core demand of Axiom 1 (Finitude) and STD-01 (Temporal Rights). The general form is the falsified ledger: when a boundary leaves out the costs, burdens, and failures needed to understand performance, accurate accounting inside it still produces a false account.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: End-to-end resolution time, including user and operator labor, is reported beside server-side processing time.
Time spent on disputes, appeals, and workarounds is budgeted and shown on operational dashboards.
entries.genealogy: Counts the human time that productivity claims leave out.

entries.title: Challenge density
entries.bodyHtml:
The rate at which challenges arrive against the capacity to answer them. Per case, procedural force is a bounded transaction; in aggregate it is a budget line. A response apparatus that is saturated is measuring the gap between the volume of error a system emits and the corrective capacity its delegation was granted with.

It matters because congestion is the point where the open circuit is usually lost. The reflexive response to volume is narrowing standing, which converts the open circuit back into a closed one exactly when the volume proves the system fails often. Density is governed by capacity decisions or scope decisions, not by eligibility decisions: sustained breaches of response clocks are a resourcing event, and an institution that meets them by narrowing who may challenge has treated a capacity signal as a permissions problem.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Challenge volume and response capacity are reported as a ratio, not as separate unread series.
A sustained breach of response clocks triggers a recorded resourcing or scope decision.
Standing was not narrowed, and no admissibility bar was raised, in direct response to a congestion breach.
entries.genealogy: Carries Law VII's per-case rule into the aggregate: the theory essay on challenge density answers the vetocracy objection with measured response capacity rather than narrower standing.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A challenge load series: volume, response capacity, and unanswered-challenge age, reported together.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A congestion breach answered with a resourcing or scope decision that is recorded and dated.
minimumEvidence.metric: Median challenge response latency and the age of the oldest unanswered challenge.

entries.title: Recourse performance
entries.bodyHtml: How well a system delivers review → reversal → remedy under realistic load and stress. It combines how fast harm is halted, how fast people are restored, and how often appeals succeed into one picture.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Recourse metrics are measured under realistic load, not only in the happy path.
A recourse failure is treated as a system defect with an owner and a fix date.
entries.genealogy: Folds the individual indicators into one end-to-end performance question.

entries.title: Reversal cost
entries.bodyHtml:
The time, money, emotional labor, documentation, and social risk required to undo an outcome. High reversal cost makes errors durable and turns “rights” into luxuries.

It is the practical face of irreversibility and the target that a reversal SLA is meant to bound.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: The cost to reverse a decision is quantified and capped.
A reversal that costs more than the harm it corrects is flagged as a design failure.
entries.genealogy: Prices the frictional barrier between a wrong state and its correction.

entries.title: Durability of error
entries.bodyHtml:
How long a wrong state persists once created, and how far it propagates (downstream systems, eligibility, reputation). A system is dangerous when it can create durable errors quickly but correct them slowly.

It is what error cascades amplify and what moral latency measures between harm and correction.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: The lifetime of a wrong state is measured from creation to correction.
Propagation paths are mapped so an error’s downstream blast radius is known.
entries.genealogy: Makes error persistence a first-class safety metric rather than a footnote.

entries.title: Dual-ledger evaluation
entries.bodyHtml:
An evaluation that scores a system on two ledgers. The first holds visible operational metrics: resolution speed, unit cost, and throughput. The second, kept independently, holds the human capacity used up, uncounted compensatory labor, and whether people keep standing to contest.

Each ledger has floors the other cannot buy out. High visible output cannot offset a failure on human depletion or suppressed rights.
examples: An AI triage audit calculates visible diagnostic speed on one ledger and nursing overtime and burnout risk on an independent audit ledger.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Evaluation reports present both operational throughput and independent audit metrics with non-compensatory scoring floors.
A high score on processing speed cannot offset an audit finding of unrecorded compensatory human labor.
entries.genealogy: Keeps human costs on a second ledger so they cannot be netted against output.

entries.title: Intrinsic performance
entries.bodyHtml:
How well an automated system or procedure performs without uncredited human compensation, shadow workarounds, or harm absorbed downstream. It measures what the system does on its own, not what it reports while people quietly prop it up.

There are two ways to find it: subtract unbudgeted human interventions from gross output, or run the system while operators follow the published protocols and nothing more.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Metrics for whether a system can still be halted, reversed, and challenged, and for what its errors cost the people who carry them.
operationalTests: Task success rates are reported for runs in which operators follow the official runbooks and make no unrecorded interventions.
Net throughput is reported after deducting the labor hours spent auditing, correcting, and appealing wrong outputs.
entries.genealogy: Answers productivity claims that rest on a falsified denominator and uncounted operator labor.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An intrinsic performance evaluation report showing error rates under automated-only processing.
minimumEvidence.behavior: Auditors running synthetic transaction suites without human intervention to establish baseline capabilities.
minimumEvidence.metric: Net autonomous task completion rate excluding downstream correction hours.

entries.title: Performance decomposition
entries.bodyHtml: The breakdown of observed performance into two parts: what the system's design delivers, and the uncredited human work that makes up the rest. As a formula: observed performance = designed capacity + human compensation. When the second term is left outside the accounting boundary, the system's apparent efficiency is overstated by that amount.
examples: An insurance claim automation system claims 98% automated clearance, but accounting reveals 35 full-time clerks manually correcting rejected formatting codes behind the scenes.
entries.scope: G. Measures & indicators. Quantifiable indicators for tracking institutional burden, correction latency, and system health.
operationalTests: Workaround hours and manual exception repair are quantified and subtracted from reported productivity gains.
Throughput is measured in a work-to-rule test, with staff following written procedure and working no off-ledger overtime, and reported beside the headline figure.
entries.genealogy: Gives the falsified denominator a formula, so the missing term can be measured.

entries.title: Adaptation externality
entries.bodyHtml: The unmeasured cost borne by the affected party or the frontline operator when a system pushes onto them the work of making an inflexible process function. That work includes vigilance, patience, error correction, and manual translation. It is the human compensation term in performance decomposition.
examples: An electronic health record system reports reduced clerical overhead for hospitals while shifting hours of uncompensated documentation and alert filtering onto physicians each day.
entries.scope: C. Measures & evaluations. Quantitative and qualitative protocols for assessing institutional strain and error propagation.
operationalTests: The gap between the institution's reported operating cost and the total time and labor needed to reach a correct outcome is calculated and reported.
Uncredited work hours for users and frontline operators are measured before and after a deployment that claims efficiency gains.
entries.genealogy: Draws on the economics of externalities, resilience engineering, and feminist social reproduction theory.

categories.heading: H. Governance & power
categories.descriptionHtml: Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Attestation
entries.bodyHtml:
The signature binding a record to a named key holder at a point in time. An attestation carries the key-holder identifier, the algorithm, the signature, and when it was produced, so that authority that cannot be attributed to a key holder is distinguishable from authority nobody signed.

It matters because delegation otherwise becomes orphaned: capability exercises the authority and no one answers for it. An attestation older than the record's last transition covers a record that no longer exists, so re-attestation at renewal is part of the discipline rather than a courtesy.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every authority grant carries signed_by, algorithm, signature, and signed_at.
A signature older than the last state transition is reported as stale, not current.
The payload digest reproduces the exact signed content.
entries.genealogy: STD-08 added the attestation to the authority grant so that the liability record answers who answers for a delegation and the attestation answers who put it in force.

minimumEvidence.artifact: Grant records carrying attestation blocks with key holder, algorithm, and signed_at.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A grant whose signature predates its last state transition is refused as evidence of the current state.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of live grants whose attestation is newer than their last transition.

entries.title: Liability record
entries.bodyHtml:
The part of a system's permission record that names who accepts liability for the automation's delays and errors, the instrument that binds them, and the exclusions they claim, called carve-outs. It exists because a system may not hide behind algorithmic error: the operating institution answers for what its delegation does.

Carve-outs are recorded before an incident rather than assembled after one. A limitation the issuer knows about is priced at deployment; the record exists so the residual risk everyone else carries is visible in the issuer's words, not the defendant's.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every grant names the party accepting liability and the instrument that binds them.
Carve-outs, caps, and exclusions appear on the record, not in a dispute.
Subcontracting does not diffuse liability: the head grant answers for every hop of a chain.
entries.genealogy: STD-01 §6.2 states the liability of automata; STD-08 gave the statement an object so the acceptance is inspectable rather than assumed.

minimumEvidence.artifact: Grant records with a liability object naming accepting party, instrument, and carve-outs.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A deployment with no recorded liability acceptance does not pass its safety-case review.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential grants with a named liability party and a recorded instrument.

entries.title: Carve-out
entries.bodyHtml:
An exclusion, cap, or condition the accepting party claims against a recorded liability. Carve-outs are recorded on the liability record rather than reserved for litigation, because the forensically useful moment to assemble an excuse is before the harm, in the issuer's words.

A carve-out on the record is a price: it states how much of the risk the liability does not cover and therefore who carries the rest. A carve-out that surfaces for the first time in a dispute is evidence of concealment rather than a term of the deal.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every carve-out claimed against a liability appears on the grant record.
The residual risk a carve-out leaves is identifiable and priced.
No carve-out appears first in a dispute.
entries.genealogy: STD-08 records carve-outs as part of the liability object so the excuse is assembled before the incident.

minimumEvidence.artifact: Liability records listing every claimed exclusion or cap with its basis.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A dispute resolved by invoking a carve-out that was never recorded counts as a governance failure.
minimumEvidence.metric: Count of carve-outs per liability record and their aggregate coverage gap.

entries.title: Delegation chain
entries.bodyHtml:
A sequence of delegations that together produce one consequential decision: an agent subcontracting to an agent, a service calling a service, across components, providers, or institutions. The agent chains standard (STD-09) treats the chain as one delegation, governed at the layer where it fails: every hop listed on the grant at the head of the chain, liability ending at the head, and one point of intervention at the boundary.

Each hop can satisfy the standards alone while the composition remains unauditable and attributed to no one. The chain exists as an object so it can be paused, challenged, and attributed as one delegation rather than as a pile of conformant parts.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The head grant enumerates every contributing delegation in execution order.
Every hop resolves to a full grant with its own scope, mode, and revocation conditions.
One intervention at the boundary halts every hop, with a receipt for the chain.
entries.genealogy: STD-09 exists because per-hop conformance does not compose: the relevant eval sits at the highest layer where harm can emerge, and for a chain that layer is the chain.

minimumEvidence.artifact: Head grants with a chain field resolving to full grant records per hop.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A boundary intervention halts every hop and emits one chain-level halt receipt.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential decisions whose chain is fully enumerated.

entries.title: Design authority
entries.bodyHtml: The accountable power to set the constraints a system operates under, choose its safeguards, and fund their enforcement. When it is clear, incentives line up, people can still challenge decisions, and responsibility does not spread until no one can intervene.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Oversight horizon
entries.bodyHtml: The distance regulators, auditors, or affected communities can see into a system’s decisions and their effects. It extends when the system shows its impact on people, its models can be traced, and its repair records are shared, and that shrinks the places where harm goes unseen.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Permission surface
entries.bodyHtml:
Everything a system is permitted to do at a given moment, recorded as a set of grants, each with the evidence behind it, its scope, its current state, and its expiry. The surface is described by authority rather than by access points: an unused grant is still part of it, and a reachable capability with no grant behind it is not part of it at all.

Every element of the surface is an authority grant that can be narrowed, suspended, or allowed to lapse, which is what makes the surface governable rather than merely documented. Comparing the surface against the capability catalog is the direct test of whether capability has outrun permission, and a wide surface makes contestability practical only when each grant in it can be challenged.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
examples: A tenant can pause automated collections, download their case record, and request human review without manager pre-approval.

entries.title: Bounded autonomy
entries.bodyHtml:
Autonomy granted only within explicit limits. Approaching or crossing a limit must escalate the case to the people who set the system's rules or to its documented outside oversight.

The limits live in an authority grant and are enforced through its grant state. Widening them is an expansion decision, not a configuration change.
examples: A claims assistant can approve payouts up to $500, but anything higher is routed to a supervisor.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Earned autonomy
entries.bodyHtml:
Autonomy that expands only after demonstrated reliability, monitoring, and accountability. What the system is permitted to do widens only as named owners and repair records show it can handle more scope.

The demonstration is evidence for widening a specific authority grant, recorded as a transition in its grant state. Reliability is the argument for an expansion decision, never a substitute for one.
examples: After six months of clean audits, the escalation bot gains approval rights for low-risk cases.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Scope discipline
entries.bodyHtml: The practice of not exceeding one’s mandate, even when doing so might appear helpful or efficient. It keeps a system within what it is permitted to do and the limits on its autonomy.
examples: A support bot refuses to access customer data outside its assigned ticket.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Right of exit
entries.bodyHtml:
The ability to leave a system without ruinous cost, retaliation, or silent lock-in. Consent means little when departure is punitive, so right of exit is a precondition for consent.

Operationally, exit requires data portability, clear closure paths, and protections against downstream penalties.

Exit is real only when it is priced. A measured substitution cost and demonstrated institutional reversibility are what separate a right of exit from a clause nobody can afford to invoke. Consent depth is the reason the pricing has to be redone: the choice made at adoption was not a choice about the dependency that grew afterward.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
examples: Workers can opt out of an automated scheduling tool and keep equivalent access to shifts while a manual process remains available.

entries.title: Externalized harm channels
entries.bodyHtml:
The pathways through which institutions push risk, cleanup, or delay onto others: contractors, users, bystanders, or future teams. Mapping these channels exposes hidden transfer mechanisms behind nominally efficient systems.

The map is used to give each channel an accountable owner and to move the burden back toward the system owner.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
examples: A platform offloads fraud remediation to merchants without funding support capacity, shifting investigation labor downstream.

entries.title: Stewardship window
entries.bodyHtml:
A negotiated period where teams pause growth work to do maintenance, close open repairs, and fix gaps in ownership.

Stewardship windows bundle maintenance windows, publish fairness and safety measures for the pause, and commit to closing items in the repair log before resuming throughput.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Stewardship
entries.bodyHtml: An explicit, ongoing role responsible for system behavior over time, with authority to pause, fix, or retire it.
examples: A named steward can pause a rollout and own the repair log.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Governance by suspension
entries.bodyHtml:
Control exercised by keeping matters unresolved long enough that time itself produces the outcome.

Governance by suspension relies on non-decisions and exploits endurance asymmetry.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Endurance asymmetry
entries.bodyHtml:
Institutions can persist indefinitely; humans cannot. This makes delay an allocation mechanism.

Endurance asymmetry underwrites continuity privilege and punitive friction.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Continuity privilege
entries.bodyHtml:
Unequal access to enforceability produced by unequal capacity to maintain standing over time (attention, health, documentation, slack).

Continuity privilege steepens the burden gradient for those without reserves.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Proxy privilege
entries.bodyHtml:
Unequal enforceability produced by unequal ability to delegate persistence (agents, intermediaries, automation).

Proxy privilege lets some parties bypass the futility threshold that others face alone.

The asymmetry becomes legible when each proxy holds a named authority grant with a visible grant state, so extending a proxy’s reach is an expansion decision rather than an unremarked advantage.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Latency-as-action
entries.bodyHtml:
The principle that delay produced predictably by system rules (queues, resets, blocked escalation, absent deadlines) is attributable power, not mere inaction.

Latency-as-action frames delay as governance and grounds decision artifacts.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Bounded duration
entries.bodyHtml:
A declared maximum time for a case to be resolved, with a stated outcome that takes effect, and can be enforced, when the time runs out.

It works alongside a stable clock, which the institution cannot reset, and time transparency, which lets the person see where their case stands.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Continuity of state
entries.bodyHtml:
A persistent cumulative case record that prevents forced repetition of validated inputs across channels, time, and teams. Continuity of state lowers administrative burden and reduces avoidable denial loops.

It protects contestability by ensuring prior evidence remains legible during escalation or transfer.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
examples: A claimant can move from chat to phone support without re-uploading documents because prior verification artifacts follow the case.

entries.title: Safe pause / status quo during pendency
entries.bodyHtml:
While a review is pending, nothing adverse happens to the person under review. A narrow emergency exception may apply, and it can itself be reviewed.

Safe pause preserves the utility window and keeps people whole during appeal.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
commonCounterfeits: “We won’t punish you” while consequences quietly accrue.

entries.title: Traceable ownership
entries.bodyHtml:
A named responsible party with authority to override automation when bounds are breached.

Traceable ownership clarifies design authority and accelerates time-to-restore.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
commonCounterfeits: Team inbox or triage queue with no override authority.

entries.title: Time transparency
entries.bodyHtml:
A person can see where their case stands: the current step, what is blocking it, the time remaining, the next decision point, and what would trigger escalation. Any progress shown is real progress.

Time transparency supports contestability and a stable clock.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
commonCounterfeits: “Status updates” with no time remaining or escalation triggers.

entries.title: Obligation continuity
entries.bodyHtml:
Whether responsibility stays attached across time, handoffs, and narrative resets instead of evaporating.

Obligation continuity depends on traceable ownership, continuity of state, and a durable repair log.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Delay as power
entries.bodyHtml:
The ability to remain wrong without consequence by stretching time (“pending,” “in review”).

Delay as power operationalizes latency-as-action and shows up in governance by suspension.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Performance-gated remedy
entries.bodyHtml:
The correction path works only if someone performs well under stress; the system treats composure as eligibility.

Performance-gated remedy undermines contestability and violates care floor guarantees.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Bindingness after contact
entries.bodyHtml:
The obligations that attach once harm is reported or help is requested, and whether they fall on the institution or on the claimant.

Bindingness after contact requires traceable ownership and a time-bounded repair log.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Recognition as solvent
entries.bodyHtml:
Being “heard” is treated as if it discharges obligation, pressuring the claimant to stop escalating without repair.

Recognition as solvent offers procedural empathy in place of the material remedies on the restitution ladder.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Unowned obligation
entries.bodyHtml:
Responsibility exists but no owner or time-bound state transition is attached; people are bounced between channels.

Unowned obligation signals missing traceable ownership and weak bounded duration.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Closure-code regime
entries.bodyHtml:
The set of person-level reason codes that convert structural scarcity into individual failure (“withdrew,” “no response,” “noncompliant”).

Closure-code regimes mask governance by suspension and normalize punitive friction.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Attrition-as-resolution
entries.bodyHtml:
An anti-pattern where drop-off is counted as success and metrics improve when people give up. Attrition-as-resolution hides unmet obligations behind completion dashboards.

It often co-occurs with endurance asymmetry and extraction by endurance, shifting repair cost onto those with the least capacity.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
examples: A benefits workflow reports higher “closure” rates after adding extra verification loops that cause applicants to abandon appeals.

entries.title: Legitimacy laundering
entries.bodyHtml:
Moral language (“we care,” “be reasonable”) substitutes for binding obligation and repair.

Legitimacy laundering offers recognition without bindingness after contact or a repair log.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Legitimacy engineering
entries.bodyHtml:
Legitimacy treated as measurable requirements rather than as a reputation: standing and remedy for the people a system decides about, a named authority on stated evidence, a halt path, and time-bounded repair.

It is the opposite of legitimacy laundering, which keeps the signals of accountability without the substance. Its center is contestability: a system is legitimate insofar as the people it decides about have standing and remedy against it. Stoppability and reversibility are what make that remedy possible.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Exit coercion
entries.bodyHtml:
“Consent” and silence extracted under duress during departures, often via NDAs, retaliation risk, or narrative erasure.

Exit coercion violates the right of exit and collapses refusal budgets.

Coercion is easiest where leaving is expensive, so the countermeasures are the ones that make leaving affordable: a measured substitution cost and maintained institutional reversibility. Where neither is maintained, consent depth does the coercing on its own and no one has to apply pressure.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Retaliation surface
entries.bodyHtml: Where the system can punish people for contesting, pausing, refusing, or exiting — through throttling, stricter scrutiny, “account review,” or service withdrawal. Mapping the retaliation surface protects contestability and the right of exit.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Teams can name every lever that can worsen a claimant’s state after an appeal is filed, including throttling, scrutiny, account review, or service withdrawal.
Safeguards document how retaliation levers are disabled or monitored during appeals.

entries.title: Non-retaliation guarantee
entries.bodyHtml: A binding commitment that contesting, pausing, refusing, or exiting will not trigger adverse treatment. A non-retaliation guarantee makes contestability and the right of exit safe to exercise.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Adverse-action rates are tracked for users who appeal versus those who do not.
Policies and interfaces explicitly state that contesting, pausing, refusing, or exiting will not trigger adverse treatment.

entries.title: Appeal integrity
entries.bodyHtml:
Appeals are judged on merits with transparent criteria, named authority, and documented outcomes — not absorbed into procedural theater. Appeal integrity ensures contestability yields real corrective action.

Strong integrity requires publishable decision artifacts, reversible outcomes, and safeguards against retaliatory handling.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The share of appeals receiving a decision artifact is tracked and published.
Appeals include named authority with overturn power rather than advisory review only.
examples: An appeals dashboard shows overturn rate, rationale categories, and median response time by decision class.

entries.title: Escalation reliability
entries.bodyHtml: Escalation paths work under load, after hours, and for novices, as shown in drills rather than in documentation. It keeps the chain of people who can stop, reverse, or repair harm intact when stress is highest.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Escalation drills hit time-to-human and time-to-decision targets across nights, weekends, and peak load.
Novice users can reach the same escalation path without privileged channels.

entries.title: Decision reversal authority
entries.bodyHtml:
A formally granted power to undo harmful decisions, not merely recommend reconsideration. Decision reversal authority turns reversibility into an enforceable capability with named ownership.

Authority should include scope boundaries, auditability, and response clocks so reversals can occur during live incidents.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: A named role has unilateral reversal power for defined classes of harm.
Policy and tooling document how reversals are executed and logged.
examples: A safety officer can immediately reverse automated account suspensions for urgent livelihood-impact cases without waiting for weekly review.

entries.title: Restitution ladder
entries.bodyHtml: A tiered remedy system that moves from apology to reversal, compensation, repair service, and systemic fix triggers. The restitution ladder ensures repair quorums stay practical and selectable.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The restitution ladder exists, is selectable in policy or tooling, and is routinely used.
Case reviews show remedies advancing beyond apologies when harm warrants compensation or repair services.

entries.title: Remedy equivalence
entries.bodyHtml:
Manual and automated channels must offer equivalent remedy outcomes, timelines, and authority. People should not be penalized for choosing accessibility, safety, or human review paths.

Remedy equivalence is measured by comparing reversal rates, escalation success, and time-to-resolution across channels.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Appeal passage rates and time-to-resolution are compared across manual and automated channels.
Policy guarantees that manual paths can reach the same remedy outcomes as automated paths.
examples: A disability accommodation appeal filed by phone has the same overturn authority and SLA as the web portal process.

entries.title: Case ownership continuity
entries.bodyHtml: Cases do not become orphaned across handoffs; ownership persists through vacations, organizational changes, or vendor transfers. Case ownership continuity strengthens traceable ownership for contested decisions.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Cases never enter a “no owner” state, and ownership transitions are logged and visible.
Handoff procedures assign a new owner with backup coverage before the previous owner exits.

entries.title: Revisable delegation
entries.bodyHtml:
Delegation of consequential work to a machine that stays tied to the evidence and beliefs that justified it, so the grant can be narrowed, suspended, or withdrawn when those change. A revisable delegation names its holder, its ceiling, what it depends on, and what would revoke it; an unrevisable one is a transfer with a delegation's name. The objects it is written in are the authority grant, the policy record it depends on, and the delegated agency the grant creates.

Revisability is the standing property. Justified delegation is the same coupling read in the present tense: whether authority, evidence, and correction capacity are all in force right now. The two are one question at two timescales. A delegation that is justified today but not revisable cannot act on tomorrow's answer.

The question it serves is how an institution can become more capable without becoming less revisable. The record shape is defined in STD-07, and the terms the delegation must keep meeting while it stands are in STD-08. The test is whether the institution can answer, for any past action, what it believed at the time, what it had authorized, and what has since changed.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every authorization record lists its revocation conditions and the beliefs it depends on.
A discrepancy that matches a revocation condition produces a revision within a declared clock.
Someone outside the system has standing to object, and the objection is answered on the record.
entries.genealogy: Ethotechnics uses revisable delegation to name the property that bounded autonomy, decision reversal authority, and meta-contestability jointly protect once an institution lets machines act on its behalf.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An authorization record carrying holder, ceiling, depends_on, and revocation conditions.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A delegation narrowed or withdrawn in response to a recorded discrepancy, with the chain visible.
minimumEvidence.metric: Time from a matching discrepancy to the revision that answers it, against the declared clock.

examples: An agent's standing deploy permission is tied to a verified staging check; when the check breaks, the permission drops to confirm-mode automatically and the log shows which record forced it.

entries.title: Authority grant
entries.bodyHtml:
The record that permits a named holder to take a bounded class of actions, for whom, under what conditions, and until when. A grant carries its scope, its evidence basis, its grant state, its expiry, and the policy records it depends on.

It matters because authority that is not written as a record cannot be reviewed, narrowed, or withdrawn. A grant that carries its dependencies and its revocation conditions is what makes the delegation a revisable delegation rather than a transfer. The grant is what makes authority drift detectable rather than merely regrettable after the fact.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every action class a system may perform maps to exactly one grant with a named holder.
Each grant states an expiry and the conditions under which it is revoked.
A grant with no revocation conditions is flagged as a transfer rather than a delegation.
entries.genealogy: Ethotechnics separates the grant from the capability so that Law I, capability does not imply authority, has an object to bind to.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An authority grant register with holder, scope, state, evidence basis, and expiry.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An attempted action outside grant scope refused and logged with the grant id.
minimumEvidence.metric: Count of live grants and share carrying a non-null expiry.

entries.title: Authority lease
entries.bodyHtml:
The stance that a grant of authority is held for a term against a renewable justification rather than owned outright. A lease expires by default, and continuing an authority grant requires fresh evidence rather than the absence of complaints.

It matters because, without a lease, silence renews a grant. Treating authority as a lease forces justified delegation to be re-established on a clock, and it puts the burden of proof on the delegation rather than on the people questioning it.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every grant has a renewal date, and passing it changes the grant state without human action.
Renewal packets cite new evidence, not the original approval.
