The renewal burden rises with the consequence class and the elapsed duration of the grant.
entries.genealogy: States Law II as a property relationship: authority is leasehold, and absence of observed failure is not payment of the rent.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A renewal record naming the evidence that justifies continuing the grant for a further term.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A grant lapsing on its renewal date because no renewal packet was filed.
minimumEvidence.metric: Median age of live grants against their declared renewal interval.

entries.title: Policy record
entries.bodyHtml:
A versioned statement of the propositions a delegation rests on: what the model does, who the population is, what the downstream process catches, and when each claim expires. Grants cite policy records rather than restating their assumptions, which is what policy as state requires.

It matters because assumptions decay silently when they are held as launch documents. Held as a record with a version and an expiry, a policy can raise a review trigger and move a grant state when the world changes. That propagation is the mechanism behind a revisable delegation: the delegation narrows because a proposition it rested on lapsed.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Each policy record states its assumptions, its evidence, its version, and its review date.
Grants reference policy records by id and version rather than paraphrasing them.
Passing a review date changes the record status and propagates to every grant that cites it.
entries.genealogy: Gives Law III an object: the propositions that justify a grant are stored where a change in the world can reach them.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A policy record with assumptions, evidence refs, version, and review date.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A lapsed policy record moving its dependent grants to review_required.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of live grants whose cited policy records are all within their review dates.

entries.title: Review trigger
entries.bodyHtml:
A rule, declared in advance, that says what happens when something is observed: when this discrepancy, expiry, or threshold occurs, this permission moves to this state, answered by this owner, within this deadline. Triggers are the wiring between monitoring and authority, and they are what give a policy record force over a grant state.

It matters because observation without a possible transition is theater. A trigger is the smallest object that makes a dashboard part of the control system rather than a record of what already happened, and it is how policy as state acquires force over a running system.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every monitored signal names the state it can change, or is marked explicitly as informational.
Each trigger names an owner and a response clock.
Silence past the clock is treated as a governance failure, not as a pending state.
entries.genealogy: Implements Law VIII: the test of an observation is whether it can change the governing state of the system.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A trigger table mapping signals to state transitions, owners, and clocks.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A monitored discrepancy producing a reconsideration record within its clock.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of monitored signals with a declared state transition, and clock breach rate.

entries.title: Correction obligation
entries.bodyHtml:
The duty an institution takes on when it delegates consequential action: to notice, stop, reverse, and repair what the delegate does. The obligation is created by the delegation itself, not by the first incident.

It matters because delegating action also delegates the ability to be wrong at scale. Stating the obligation alongside the authority grant is what makes a shortfall in correction capacity visible before it is needed rather than during an incident.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Each grant states the corrections its holder owes: which harms, notified how, reversed by whom.
Correction obligations are reviewed whenever the grant's scope or population changes.
An obligation with no funded capacity behind it is recorded as an open governance risk.
entries.genealogy: States Law IV as an object attached to the grant, so correction is authorized at the same moment as action.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A correction obligation clause on each grant, naming harms, owners, and clocks.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A scope increase blocked until the matching correction obligation was resourced.
minimumEvidence.metric: Count of stated obligations without a funded capacity owner.

entries.title: Preserved capacity
entries.bodyHtml:
An institutional capability deliberately maintained so the institution can still question, replace, or withdraw a system: retained expertise, a working manual path, independent records, a viable alternative supplier. Preserved capacities are named, owned, and funded even while idle, and they are kept honest by withdrawal rehearsal.

It matters because these are the first capacities efficiency removes. Their erosion is a governance event rather than a saving, since it is the mechanism by which a system consumes the conditions of its own contestability, destroys institutional reversibility, and ends in institutional capture. Registered capacities also decay quietly through capacity depreciation, which is why exercise dates rather than register entries are the evidence.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Preserved capacities are listed with an owner and a budget line, separate from the system's own budget.
Any proposal that reduces one is reviewed as a governance change, not as an efficiency measure.
Each capacity is exercised on a cadence so that its continued existence is demonstrated.
entries.genealogy: Gives Law XII its object: the capacities an institution needs in order to question, replace, or withdraw a consequential system.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A preserved capacity register with owners, budget lines, and exercise dates.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A cost reduction rejected or amended because it would erode a preserved capacity.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of registered capacities exercised within their declared interval.

entries.title: Corrective standing
entries.bodyHtml:
The recognized capacity of someone who bears a system's errors to start a correction. Their challenge must be received, answered by a named responder, and judged against a stated standard, and it must be able to change the system's state. Standing is proportional to exposure and carries procedural force rather than veto.

It matters because contestability without standing is a suggestion box. Standing is what converts the experience of harm into an event the governing system has to process, and it is operationalized by a standing mechanism.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Standing is declared per decision class rather than granted informally on request.
A challenge from someone with standing produces a dated response from a named party.
At least one successful challenge in the period changed a policy or grant, not only an outcome.
entries.genealogy: States Law VII in its Method-scoped form: exposure generates standing, and standing is procedural force, not control over the institution.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A standing declaration per decision class, naming who may challenge what.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A challenge raised by an affected party that changed a grant or policy state.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of challenges answered within clock, and share producing a state change.

entries.title: Standing mechanism
entries.bodyHtml:
The records and procedures that turn a right to challenge a decision into one people can use. It keeps a register of who may challenge which kinds of decision, including the people who bear the system's errors. It also names the admissible evidence, the responder, the deadline, the standard of review, and the state transitions a successful challenge can produce.

It matters because corrective standing declared without a mechanism can be neither exercised nor audited. The mechanism is the part of contestability an auditor can inspect: named responders, real clocks, and recorded outcomes.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The register, responder, deadline, and standard of review are published, not held internally.
The set of possible outcomes includes at least one that changes system state.
Non-retaliation is attested and monitored for the parties who use the mechanism.
entries.genealogy: The mechanism side of Law VII, and the amendment surface for STD-02 where standard of review and state transitions are added.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A published standing mechanism specification with register, responder, clock, and outcomes.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A challenge routed through the mechanism and answered by the named responder on time.
minimumEvidence.metric: Challenge volume, response-clock breach rate, and outcome distribution.

entries.title: Procedural force
entries.bodyHtml:
The property of a challenge that obliges a response and can change a state, as distinct from a veto that stops action outright. A challenge with procedural force must be received, answered on a clock, and capable of producing a transition; it need not prevail.

It matters because the usual objection to standing is fear of veto. Procedural force is the narrower claim that keeps corrective standing workable, and it is the difference between contestability and consultation.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every challenge channel names what must happen on receipt and by when.
The possible outcomes are enumerated, and at least one is a state change rather than an explanation.
A challenge that is answered but produces no possible transition is recorded as consultation.
entries.genealogy: Draws the line Law VII draws: standing is procedural force, not veto, so the claim survives contact with operational reality.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A challenge specification listing obligations on receipt and enumerated outcomes.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A challenge that did not prevail but still produced a recorded reconsideration.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of challenges producing a recorded state transition of any kind.

entries.title: Consent depth
entries.bodyHtml:
The distinction between consenting to enter a dependency and consenting to every degree of dependency its operation produces. Adoption is one choice, made once, under one set of alternatives; depth is what accumulates afterward without any further choice being offered.

The choice at adoption helps manufacture the constrained choice set later. Data accumulates, collaborators organize around the system, alternatives disappear, and the adopter's own competence atrophies, so “you chose this” stops describing the present relationship. Enumerating affected parties at adoption does not close the set either, because people become exposed later without ever having been asked. Bound by STD-02 §10.1 and §10.2.

It matters because standing is usually rationed by original consent. Depth is why corrective standing has to reach anyone who became an error-bearing party after adoption, and why a deepened dependency is where exit coercion operates with nobody applying pressure, leaving a right of exit that is formally intact and practically spent.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The affected-party set is reopened at each review rather than fixed at adoption.
Adverse movement in exposure score, substitution cost, or reversibility level since consent is disclosed to the consenting party.
The operator can name the last material deepening of the dependency and show what was disclosed at the time.
entries.genealogy: Separates the Law VII question of who holds standing from the moment of adoption, so consent cannot be used to price a relationship it no longer describes.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A consent record paired with a dated dependency trend showing exposure score, substitution cost, and reversibility level at consent and now.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A disclosure sent to consenting parties when the dependency deepened materially, ahead of the next renewal.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of material deepenings disclosed within a stated interval, and share of parties who became affected after adoption who hold standing.

entries.title: Constitutional governance
entries.bodyHtml:
A way of governing automated systems built on recorded grants of authority, limits on jurisdiction, a recognized right for the people who bear errors to challenge them, and enforceable recourse. It is set against behavioral alignment. Alignment asks whether an automated system intends what its creators intend. Constitutional governance asks what authority the system holds, what happens when it is wrong or incomplete, and who has standing to compel correction.

Constitutional governance starts from three premises. Authority cannot rest on the absence of observed failure. Evidence and authority must stay coupled. A system's politics show in the rights people hold when its model fails.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Authority is bounded in an explicit grant object with expiration dates and invalidation conditions rather than open-ended permissions.
Error-bearing parties hold procedural standing to initiate review and compel state transitions when systems fail.
entries.genealogy: Distinguishes architectural authority control from behavioral alignment in autonomous and delegated systems.

entries.title: Corrigibility rent
entries.bodyHtml:
Power gained because others cannot cheaply make you answer for being wrong. A conventional rent comes from holding a scarce position; a corrigibility rent comes from holding a position whose wrongness is expensive to establish — through impossible complaint procedures, proprietary evidence, inaccessible records, inscrutable systems, monopoly expertise, catastrophic exit costs, or appeals that arrive only after the harm has become irreversible.

It matters because it names the portion of authority the framework systematically erodes: not power as such, but the part that survives only because contradiction has been made costly, ineffectual, or invisible. The presumption it reverses is the audit's center of gravity: an institution that wants consequential authority must build and maintain the conditions under which its own wrongness can be established and remedied.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The cost a challenger bears to establish the institution was wrong is measured and compared with the institution's stake in the outcome.
Records that would establish wrongness are held by the party whose wrongness they would establish.
The meta-question — who decides what happens after someone says no — has a named, answerable owner.
entries.genealogy: Names the rent the casebook's failures were collecting: Robodebt, Horizon, and the childcare-benefits scandal all priced their wrongness beyond their challengers' reach.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A contestation-cost inventory: what a challenger must spend, in time, evidence, and money, to establish an error.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A wrongness-establishing route exercised by a challenge and producing a remedy within the challenger's budget.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential decisions whose error can be established by the error-bearing party at proportionate cost.

entries.title: Insulation
entries.bodyHtml:
Insulation keeps the harm a decision causes from reaching anyone who can change the rule. Where it holds, the people harmed cope, and their coping is read as proof the rule works. It takes nine forms:

  • Material: someone else pays.
  • Organizational: frontline workers absorb failures before they reach leadership.
  • Epistemic: the institution measures completed outcomes but not the work it took to complete them.
  • Procedural: appeals exist but take extraordinary time, persistence, expertise, or money.
  • Temporal: consequences arrive after the decision-maker has moved on.
  • Social: those who govern rarely meet those who absorb.
  • Legal: responsibility is fragmented or unenforceable.
  • Statistical: harm is spread so thin that no single event looks consequential.
  • Adaptive: the affected people get so good at compensating that the failure never shows.

It shields the rule-maker from consequence, not only from the sight of suffering. It needs three things together: costs are displaced, feedback is weak, and authority stays where it was. The side insulated from a mismatch leaves the other side to adapt. The better the other side adapts, the less the failure shows, and the more secure the insulated side becomes. The loop runs from bad fit to human adaptation, apparent success, institutional approval, and wider authority. It is the loop the workaround presumption is meant to break.

Not all insulation is bad. Judges may need insulation from immediate political pressure, scientists from popularity, civil servants from retaliation, and minorities from majorities. The line falls between insulation from improper pressure and insulation from evidence, accountability, and consequence. The design question is which one is being preserved.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: For each decision class, the institution can name what travels back when it is wrong, and the channel it travels through.
Absorbed failures are counted as correction events rather than as successful operations.
Insulation from pressure and insulation from consequence are distinguished, and only the first is preserved.
entries.genealogy: The closed circuit the theory essay on insulation describes: costs are displaced, feedback is weak, and authority is preserved.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A feedback map per decision class: who absorbs the mismatch, what reaches the rule-maker, and what is filtered.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An absorbed failure that reached the rule-maker and produced a rule or category change.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential decision classes where an absorbed failure reached the rule-maker within a stated clock.

entries.title: Consequential contradiction
entries.bodyHtml:
The capacity of the world a system governs to force it to reconsider — not merely to complain. Contradiction is consequential when the party bearing the mismatch can make it travel: into the record, the rule, the category, or the jurisdiction that produced it. Domination, in this frame, is power insulated from consequential contradiction: the institution defines the relevant reality, acts on its definition, pushes the residual burden downward, controls what counts as evidence against itself, and cannot be forced to revise by those it gets wrong.

It matters because procedural openness is not the test. A system can receive every complaint and learn nothing — the exception absorption mechanism — and an arrangement can be democratic, public, or participatory and still closed. The test is whether contradiction has state-changing force, which is what the corrective standing register and Law XII's preservation duties exist to secure.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Contradiction from an affected party can change a rule, category, or authority object, not only their own case.
Disagreement is not auto-classified as user error, anomalous input, or noise without a route that can overturn that classification.
The institution can name the last external contradiction that changed its categories.
entries.genealogy: States the positive form of the domination definition: power is legitimate to the extent it remains exposed to being wrong.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A revision record naming the external contradiction that produced each category or rule change.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A challenge that changes an upstream object rather than only the challenger's outcome.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of rule or category changes traceable to external contradiction rather than internal review.

entries.title: Halt stratification
entries.bodyHtml:
Halt authority tiered by blast radius, so that the power to stop grows with the size of what is stopped. A frontline operator pausing one case, a supervisor halting a queue, and a steward stopping a system use different instruments, with different restoration paths, notification duties, and evidence demands. Stratification is what keeps per-case procedural force from becoming system-wide friction.

It matters because veto-point proliferation — the standing objection to contestability — is what happens when every party holds the same maximal instrument and no one holds a graduated one. Tiering does not remove halt points; it prices them: the power to stop scales with the size of what is being stopped, and the smallest tiers stay cheap enough that people use them.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Each halt tier names who can fire it, what it stops, and the restoration path at that tier.
A tier-1 halt can be used without escalating to a tier-3 authority.
Restoration capacity is provisioned at each tier, not only at the top.
entries.genealogy: The graduated answer to the vetocracy objection: the theory essay on challenge density argues for pricing halt points by blast radius rather than removing them.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A halt tier register: tiers, authorized roles, blast radius, restoration path, and notification duty per tier.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A halt used at a low tier that resolves without escalation to a higher tier.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of halts resolved at the tier where they originated.

entries.title: Admission gate
entries.bodyHtml:
The authorization decision that precedes any grant: whether the system should act at all. An admission gate records the evidence reviewed, the scope considered, and the outcome — including deliberate non-use, which is a decision with reasons and a date, not an absence. A system refused admission has not failed; the refusal is the gate working.

It matters because capability without authority is Law I's object, but the law has a step before the grant that is easy to skip: the evaluation of whether the delegation should exist. Skipping the gate converts a governance question into a momentum question, where the system runs because someone built it and stopping now is more expensive than starting was.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: A consequential deployment has a recorded admission decision with evidence and a named decider.
Deliberate non-use is a recorded outcome with reasons, revisitable on a clock.
"Not yet" and "never" are distinguishable in the record, with different review conditions.
entries.genealogy: Operationalizes Law I at its earliest moment: capability is discovered and cataloged, authority is granted — and the grant decision itself can be no.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An admission decision record: evidence reviewed, scope considered, outcome, and reasons.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A deployment refused admission with the refusal basis recorded and a review condition named.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential deployments with a recorded admission decision.

entries.title: Dependence reciprocity
entries.bodyHtml:
The duties an institution owes to a population that has come to rely on its system. Dependence runs both ways: the institution owes notice when the dependency deepens, preservation of exit and alternatives, and continuity obligations at withdrawal. Treating a population's reliance as license to direct it is a conversion — a fact about dependence turned into an unauthorized permission — and reciprocity is the refusal of that conversion.

It matters because the dependency ledger as usually written records what the institution needs in order to withdraw, and stops there. Reciprocity completes the picture: the crumple zone is not only absorbing cost, it is holding reliance the institution benefits from, and reliance held is a claim, not a resource.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Dependents are told when their reliance on the system deepens materially.
Withdrawal from a depended-on system carries continuity obligations with dates and owners.
Dependents' claims on the system are recorded with the same standing as the institution's claims on them.
entries.genealogy: Completes Law V: dependence converts technical risk into structural risk, and the conversion runs in the direction of the dependent as well as the institution.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A reciprocity register: dependents, what their reliance holds, and the duties owed at withdrawal.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A material deepening of dependency disclosed to dependents before it takes effect.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of dependency changes with dependents notified before the change.

entries.title: Corrective power
entries.bodyHtml:
The effective capacity of affected people to make an arrangement change when its demands become unreasonable: to force reconsideration, reversal, or rule revision, not merely to complain. It is the exercised form of corrective standing — standing names the right; corrective power names whether exercising it can alter the system's governing state.

It matters because it is the second term in the discipline's evaluation formula, alongside outcome and burden: what an arrangement accomplishes, what accomplishing it requires from people, and what power those people hold over those requirements. A system whose corrections are nominal scores high on the first term and low on the third, which what outcomes hide argues is exactly the failure a pure outcome orientation cannot see.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Affected people can produce a state transition in the arrangement, not only a recorded complaint.
The cost of exercising correction is measured against the capacity of those who must bear it.
Corrective power survives the dependence that justified it being engineered away.
entries.genealogy: Completes the evaluation formula of the outcomes critique: standing made measurable as force rather than as a register entry.

entries.title: Contestability as the legitimacy hinge
entries.bodyHtml: A system is legitimate insofar as affected parties have standing, voice, and remedy against its decisions and actions. Contestability is the hinge on which legitimacy turns; legitimacy laundering is the attempt to substitute its appearance for its substance.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: A legitimacy claim is traceable to a standing mechanism, not to messaging.
Loss of remedy is scored as loss of legitimacy, not as an operational detail.
entries.genealogy: States the democratic premise that ties legitimacy to enforceable remedy.

entries.title: Maintenance budgets are legitimacy budgets
entries.bodyHtml:
The capacity to monitor, review, and repair is a political and organizational legitimacy input, not overhead. An institution that cannot afford maintenance is running down a debt it will collect as illegitimacy.

Unfunded repair is unfunded legitimacy.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Review and repair capacity is budgeted alongside feature work.
A maintenance cut is evaluated as a legitimacy cut, not a cost saving.
entries.genealogy: Reclassifies upkeep from operational expense to the currency of legitimacy.

entries.title: Receipts-by-default as a legitimacy interface
entries.bodyHtml:
People should automatically get “what happened” records: actions taken, permissions used, reasons, and accountable owners. A liability record or attestation is not a favor; it is the default output of an accountable act.

Receipts make recordkeeping symmetric instead of a lever held only by the institution.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every consequential action produces a receipt without being requested.
A receipt names an accountable owner and a clock for the next step.
entries.genealogy: Elevates receipts from a transparency nicety to a governance default.

entries.title: Sovereignty as constraint-imposition capacity
entries.bodyHtml: Sovereignty is the ability to impose enforceable constraints on infrastructure operating in your territory. Without it, design authority belongs to whoever owns the stack, and path dependence locks in their defaults.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: A jurisdiction can bind foreign infrastructure to local remedy and audit rules.
Constraint-imposition capacity is measured, not assumed from legal text.
entries.genealogy: Reframes sovereignty as an engineering capacity, not a legal claim.

entries.title: Standards wars as recourse wars
entries.bodyHtml: Global competition shifts to whose regimes for auditability, liability, and redress become default through supply chains and procurement. The war is not over features but over whose restitution and governability rules travel with the product.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Procurement criteria weight redress and auditability, not only performance.
A standard is judged by the remedy it binds, not the language it adopts.
entries.genealogy: Reads international standards competition as competition over enforceable recourse.

entries.title: Democratic vs coercive governability
entries.bodyHtml: Governance infrastructure can enable either rights-preserving contestability or scaled conduct control, depending on who has standing and remedy. Governability is neutral; its direction is set by whether standing is distributed or concentrated.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The distribution of standing is stated and measurable.
A governability claim specifies whose remedy it protects.
entries.genealogy: Splits governability along the axis that determines whether it serves or coerces.

entries.title: Bindingness
entries.bodyHtml:
The degree to which a system’s outputs create enforceable obligations — deadlines, duties, remedies, or reversals — rather than mere communications. Bindingness is the difference between “we received your request” and “we must decide by Friday or you win.”

It is the property that bindingness after contact describes at the moment of interaction, and that binding clocks make time-bound.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: An output is classified as binding or non-binding on its face.
A binding output names the obligation it creates and the authority that enforces it.
entries.genealogy: Makes enforceability the defining property of an institutional utterance.

entries.title: Non-bindingness / nonbindingness
entries.bodyHtml:
The condition where a system can interact, respond, and even apologize without being compelled to change state. Non-bindingness is power without accountability: activity without obligation.

It is the substrate on which delay as power and unearned closure operate, and the opposite of bindingness.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: A response is scored by whether it can change state, not by how helpful it sounds.
Activity that cannot bind is flagged as non-binding rather than counted as remedy.
entries.genealogy: Names the default posture of institutions that prefer communication to correction.

entries.title: Standing (vs belief)
entries.bodyHtml:
Standing is the recognized right to make the system bind itself to engage, decide, and remedy — regardless of whether your story is believed, liked, or emotionally legible. “Belief” is narrative validation; standing is enforceable access to decision power.

Corrective standing is the test: can this person force a correction, or only be heard?
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Access to remedy does not depend on being believed or found sympathetic.
Standing is granted by rule and survives disagreement over the claimant’s narrative.
entries.genealogy: Separates enforceable access from narrative validation, the core distinction of the remedy vocabulary.

entries.title: Binding authority
entries.bodyHtml:
A person or role that can change the underlying state and is obligated to respond. Binding authority is not “a human is involved”; it is a human with power + duty + traceable accountability.

It is what distinguishes real review from a human-in-the-loop legitimacy artifact, and what decision reversal authority requires.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every review stage names a role that can change state, not merely comment.
The accountable owner is traceable from the decision to the record.
entries.genealogy: Defines the authority threshold that separates remedy from review theater.

entries.title: Evidence parity
entries.bodyHtml:
A condition where affected people have a fair chance to meet the evidentiary burden — access to the relevant facts, rules, and records — rather than being asked to prove things the institution can’t or won’t disclose. Without evidence parity, appeals become theater.

It is the answer to evidence burden ceilings and evidence recycling.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The institution discloses the facts it used, before the claimant must respond.
An evidentiary burden is matched to what the claimant could reasonably access.
entries.genealogy: Makes fairness a property of access to evidence, not of procedure alone.

entries.title: Authority chain
entries.bodyHtml: The mapping of who can change what state, at which stage, under what constraints. Authority chains determine whether escalation is real. They are built from authority grants and leases along a delegation chain.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every state change traces to a named authority at a named stage.
A broken authority chain (a stage with no one able to change state) is a defect.
entries.genealogy: Renders the structure of escalation explicit so it can be audited.

entries.title: Authority mutation
entries.bodyHtml:
A pattern where escalation changes how the institution speaks without changing who has power to reverse outcomes. Authority mutates when the channel upgrades (more polite, more official, more complex) but the underlying ability to bind remains absent.

It is the specific failure of escalation reliability, and the cousin of authority drift.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Escalation is scored by change in binding power, not change in tone or channel.
A channel upgrade without a power upgrade is flagged as mutation, not progress.
entries.genealogy: Names the substitution of surface escalation for real escalation.

entries.title: Defaults (as governance)
entries.bodyHtml:
The idea that the baseline state — what happens if nobody intervenes — is a primary allocator of outcomes and costs. Defaults govern by deciding who must spend time, attention, and stamina to avoid harm.

They are the silent partner of auto-close, auto-renew, auto-share, and the enemy of meaningful control.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every default is audited for who bears the cost of escaping it.
A default is chosen by the party who would bear its harm, not only its benefit.
entries.genealogy: Elevates the default from a UX detail to a governance instrument.

entries.title: Procedural caste
entries.bodyHtml:
A stratification system where people are divided by their ability to force binding action: who can start clocks, reach authorities, obtain reversals, and make claims legible. It is a caste system of enforceability, not worth.

It is produced by procedural burden priced as access and sustained by access cliffs and stamina pricing.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Enforceability is measured as a distribution across people, not a binary.
A procedural barrier is audited for who it sorts out of remedy.
entries.genealogy: Recasts procedural friction as a mechanism of social stratification.

entries.title: Escalation (without authority)
entries.bodyHtml:
A channel change that does not increase binding power — more forms, more tiers, more waiting — while the underlying decision remains unchangeable. It is escalation as delay management, not remedy.

It is the lived form of authority mutation and a vehicle for delay as power.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Escalation that cannot reach a decision-reversal authority is not counted as recourse.
Tier counts are not confused with binding-power counts.
entries.genealogy: Distinguishes moving up a channel from moving toward a binding decision.

entries.title: Redress
entries.bodyHtml:
The set of mechanisms that can correct harm: appeal, review, reversal, compensation, restoration. Redress is real when it is time-bound and reaches binding authority.

It is the umbrella over the restitution ladder, remedy equivalence, and decision reversal authority.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every harm type has a mapped redress path with a clock and an owner.
A redress path is tested end to end, not described in policy.
entries.genealogy: Unifies the correction mechanisms under a single time-bound standard.

entries.title: Override path
entries.bodyHtml:
A defined mechanism that can supersede the default workflow when the default would cause harm: human escalation with real authority, emergency reversal, or exception handling with deadlines. Override paths are where a stated commitment to people becomes a mechanism. Override paths require an ethical load path that carries the intervention to an accountable authority.

They are the practical form of intervention specification and the release valve on safe pause.

Where an ethical interrupt fires, the override path is its resolution route, and a lane that names who may intervene without resolving to the specification is a route in name only.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every default workflow has a named override with a deadline.
An override changes the underlying state; a changed conversation alone does not count.
entries.genealogy: Converts good intentions into a defined, enforceable escape hatch.

entries.title: Structured exit
entries.bodyHtml:
An exit process designed to protect the leaver: clear steps, data portability, timelines, anti-retaliation constraints, and closure that doesn’t require ongoing performance. Structured exit turns leaving into a governed pathway instead of an endurance test.

It is the machinery behind the right of exit, and the answer to exit cost and exit coercion.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Leaving has bounded steps, a deadline, and portability, not open-ended performance.
Exit carries a non-retaliation guarantee rather than reputational risk.
entries.genealogy: Makes exit a governed right rather than a test of endurance.

entries.title: Paywalled rights
entries.bodyHtml:
When access to contestation, speed, or binding review is effectively purchased — through fees, premium support, lawyers, consultants, or time flexibility. Rights exist, but only for those who can pay in money or stamina.

It is the price form of the access cliff and of stamina pricing.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Access to remedy is not gated by payment or discretionary free time.
A right that requires a professional intermediary to exercise is flagged as paywalled.
entries.genealogy: Exposes the economic gate that turns formal rights into practical privileges.

entries.title: Logs-as-power
entries.bodyHtml:
The idea that control over records — what is logged, who can see it, what counts as evidence — shapes who can contest outcomes. Recordkeeping is governance.

It is why attestation and the liability record matter, and why evidence parity is a rights question.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The evidentiary record is accessible to the affected party by default.
What is (and is not) logged is itself an accountable design decision.
entries.genealogy: Makes the log a site of power rather than a technical afterthought.

entries.title: Audit trail
entries.bodyHtml:
A trace of events and decisions — what happened, when, by whom, under what rule — used for accountability. Audit trails matter only if they connect to reversal power.

They are the raw material of the liability record and the policy record, and feed traceable ownership.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every consequential state change leaves a trace naming owner, rule, and time.
The trail reaches a decision-reversal authority rather than dead-ending in a log.
entries.genealogy: Binds recordkeeping to its purpose: making correction possible.

entries.title: Administrative reality
entries.bodyHtml:
The world as the system recognizes it: what counts, what is recordable, what triggers action. Administrative reality often diverges from lived reality.

It is the boundary drawn by legibility, the gate that harm receipts must cross, and the field in which object formation either succeeds or fails.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: A lived harm can be tested for whether it exists in the administrative record.
The divergence between lived and administrative reality is measured, not denied.
entries.genealogy: Names the recognition boundary that determines what can be contested.

entries.title: Contract of adhesion
entries.bodyHtml:
A take-it-or-leave-it contract offered by a more powerful party where negotiation is impossible; a common substrate for coerced “choice.” It is the legal form of coercive consent.

Where adhesion is total, consent depth is zero and refusability is forfeited by signing.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The power asymmetry behind a contract is measured, not assumed away.
Terms that are unavoidable are audited as defaults, not as negotiated consent.
entries.genealogy: Imports the contract-law concept that underlies much coerced “choice.”

entries.title: NDA retaliation / narrative erasure
entries.bodyHtml:
Mechanisms that suppress exit stories — legal threats, informal retaliation, reputational control — preventing systems from being held accountable by shared evidence. They extend the retaliation surface beyond the employment relationship.

They are what a non-retaliation guarantee must cancel, and a driver of exit coercion.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Silencing mechanisms are named and countered, not treated as neutral legal practice.
Exit stories can be shared without retaliation, by design and by rule.
entries.genealogy: Connects legal silencing to the erasure of the evidence that remedies require.

entries.title: Decision threshold
entries.bodyHtml:
The score, cut-off, or confidence floor that decides whether an action runs unattended, goes to a person, or is refused. In a deployment gated by a classifier or a typed decision model, the threshold is where authority is conferred: the model proposes, and the number decides what the institution lets it do.

It matters because thresholds are usually held as configuration, tuned once against one model version and never recorded as a decision. STD-08 §2.6 holds a decision threshold as a policy record whose assumptions name the labeled cases, model version, question schema, and option order it was set against, with a review trigger on any change to them. Where the threshold also chooses what reaches a reviewer, it is part of the intervention specification.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every threshold that routes a consequential action resolves to a policy record with provenance, assumptions, review triggers, and an expiry.
The policy record names the model version, question schema, and option order the threshold was tuned against, and the production values match it.
A change to the model version, schema, or option order moves the threshold's policy record to review_required.
entries.genealogy: Gives Law III an object at the point where typed decision models locate authority: the evidence for a threshold is the labeled data and the model version it was set against, and it decays when either changes.

references.label: Typed decision models and where their authority lives

minimumEvidence.artifact: A policy record for each routing threshold, naming its tuning set, pinned model version, schema, and option order.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A model upgrade or option reorder moving the threshold's policy record to review_required before it gates another action.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of routing thresholds backed by a policy record pinned to the model version in production.

entries.title: Shaping hop
entries.bodyHtml:
A component that routes, orders, ranks, filters, or drops the cases, inputs, or evidence a consequential decision is made on, without making the decision itself. Triage classifiers, retrieval filters, priority routers, and model routers that pick which delegate decides are all shaping hops.

It matters because each call looks like plumbing, so none is granted, while together they decide whose case waits, which evidence the decider never sees, and which applicant reaches a person. STD-09 §1.5 enumerates shaping hops in the delegation chain and assesses their consequence in aggregate. STD-09 §1.6 treats a hop that selects the delegate at run time as a delegation over its whole range, so every delegate it can choose is granted and each decision record names the one that decided.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Every component that routes, ranks, filters, or drops a consequential decision's inputs appears in the head grant's chain.
Each shaping hop's consequence is reported in aggregate, such as wait times or evidence excluded, not per call.
Decision records name the delegate a router selected, and the router's full range is enumerated.
entries.genealogy: Extends Law I one boundary further: capability that shapes a decision through a hop nobody granted is capability outrunning authority, however small each output looks.

references.label: Typed decision models and where their authority lives

minimumEvidence.artifact: A chain enumeration that lists every routing, ranking, and filtering component, with the grant each runs under.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A new triage classifier or router candidate recorded as a chain event before it runs.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of decision records that name every hop that shaped them, including the delegate a router selected.

entries.title: Confidence-gated execution
entries.bodyHtml:
An arrangement in which a model's confidence decides whether an action runs unattended, goes to a person, or is refused. It is sold as oversight that scales: high-confidence cases run, and people see only the uncertain ones.

It matters because it moves both authority and review into a number. The threshold confers the authority, so STD-08 §2.6 holds it as a decision threshold policy. The threshold also chooses the reviewer's queue, so STD-08 §3.6 makes it part of the intervention specification and sends a sample of the confident cases to review too, because a queue fed only with uncertain cases cannot detect a confident error. Without both, the arrangement is human oversight in name only.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: The routing threshold resolves to a pinned policy record and is named on the intervention specification.
A declared share of decisions that ran unattended reaches review, and its reversal rate is reported apart from the routed queue.
The record states whether the reviewer sees the model's score.
entries.genealogy: Applies Law IX to review queues selected by a score: a person who only ever sees the cases the model was unsure of cannot alter what the model was sure of.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An intervention specification with a routing block naming the threshold policy, whether the score is shown, and the unreviewed sample.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A threshold change opening a reconsideration of the intervention specification.
minimumEvidence.metric: Reversal rate in the sample of decisions that ran unattended, reported apart from the routed queue.

entries.title: Systemic refusal
entries.bodyHtml:
A collective decision by operators, caseworkers, or the people a system decides about to stop absorbing its failures. They stop the uncounted work that hides the failures, and the cost of the system's errors shows up in the institution's own records as it happens.

Refusing to absorb the failures is not obstruction. It puts the defects on the institution's record, where someone has to answer for them and repair them.
examples: Claims examiners decline to fix garbled automated decision notices by hand, routing them back to the automated pipeline and surfacing the defect to executive leadership.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.
operationalTests: Operators can keep to documented procedures and standard hours, and send unhandled edge cases to formal escalation queues, without penalty.
When operators stop absorbing failures, the failures show up in the institution's own metrics and are assigned to someone who can fix the design.
entries.genealogy: Compare work-to-rule, where staff follow written procedure and nothing more, and the andon cord, which lets any worker stop a production line.

entries.title: Corrective standing as epistemic admissibility
entries.bodyHtml: The requirement that friction and contradiction from affected people enter the institutional record as evidence. Once recorded, they must be able to change the model or category that produced them. They are not dismissed as user error, settled as one-off grievances, or absorbed by frontline staff.
examples: A tenant portal automatically records repeated repair escalations as structural building defects that trigger rent escrow reviews, rather than closing tickets upon dispatch.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Concepts governing authority boundaries, delegation protocols, and institutional answerability.
operationalTests: Affected parties can log a contradiction directly in the system of record, without a gatekeeper in between.
Aggregated contradiction logs trigger mandatory evidentiary re-evaluations under STD-07.
entries.genealogy: Draws on epistemic injustice (Fricker) and requisite variety (Ashby).

entries.title: Ethical circuit breakers
entries.bodyHtml: Automated stops that trip when a risk indicator crosses a set point: a surge in appeals, a bias metric, or a growing backlog of harm not yet repaired. They are the safety counterpart to financial circuit breakers.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

entries.title: Graceful rollback lanes
entries.bodyHtml: Prepared routes to revert harmful decisions while preserving dignity, evidence, and service continuity. They lower the share of actions that cannot be undone and shorten the time to restore people.
entries.scope: H. Governance & power. Structures that decide who holds authority, on what grant and for how long, and who can intervene.

categories.heading: I. Friction & flow
categories.descriptionHtml: Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.

entries.title: Protective friction
entries.bodyHtml:
Friction added on purpose to slow a harmful process, so the lag between harm and response stays within safe bounds. Protective friction inserts checkpoints where speed would otherwise amplify risk.

It should be targeted and proportional: enough to prevent harm, not enough to create punitive burden.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.
examples: High-risk account changes require a second authenticated confirmation before execution.

entries.title: Punitive friction
entries.bodyHtml:
Friction that punishes users through unnecessary loops, opaque requirements, or repeated proof demands. Punitive friction often masks extraction by endurance as policy.

Unlike protective friction, it raises cost without improving safety or repair outcomes.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.
examples: A dispute process forces users through multiple redundant forms before any human review is allowed.

entries.title: Procedural burden as price
entries.bodyHtml:
Paperwork and “friction” are not incidental; they are rationing mechanisms that should be capped, disclosed, or penalized.

Procedural burden as price exposes punitive friction and steepens the burden gradient.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.

entries.title: Dignity friction
entries.bodyHtml:
Friction that preserves autonomy, such as double checks on irreversible actions and plain-language confirmation states. Dignity friction helps people understand consequences before commitment without shaming them for caution.

It differs from punitive friction because the cost is proportional to risk and paired with clear pathways forward.
examples: Before account deletion, the interface requires a brief confirmation with restore options and support contact details.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.

entries.title: Velocity friction
entries.bodyHtml:
Friction added specifically to prevent runaway system behaviors in high-speed workflows. Velocity friction creates deliberate pauses before scale multiplies harm.

Common mechanisms include rate limits, staged rollouts, and mandatory human checkpoints tied to ethical interrupts.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.
examples: A recommendation engine rollout is throttled by cohort with auto-pause triggers when harmful engagement signals rise.

entries.title: Safety valve
entries.bodyHtml:
A deliberate release point that lets people slow, pause, or reroute automation before harm compounds.

Safety valves pair stoppability with dignity friction so flows with serious consequences default to reversible states and route to humans without penalty.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.

entries.title: Consent journey
entries.bodyHtml:
The points where a person learns what a system will do, grants or refuses permission, and can revise that choice later.

A strong one previews future uses and lets the person approve, defer, or block them, shows what the system is permitted to do, and lets people pause or leave without losing access or service.

A journey that ends at adoption misses consent depth: the dependency keeps deepening after the permission was granted, and the choice has to be reopened rather than remembered.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.

entries.title: Humane friction
entries.bodyHtml:
Slowdowns placed across a whole workflow so the process slows only where risk, irreversibility, or pressure to coerce is high. It combines protective, dignity, and velocity friction.

Each point of friction can be explained, removed, and measured, and it reduces later harm without trapping people in needless process.
examples: A lending flow adds extra verification only for high-risk decisions and offers an accessible appeal path when checks block approval.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.

entries.title: Appropriate friction
entries.bodyHtml: Deliberate slowdowns or checkpoints inserted where harm would be costly or irreversible. It treats slowing fast automated steps and automatic halts as safety features.
examples: High-risk data exports require a second reviewer before completion.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.

entries.title: Frictionless harm
entries.bodyHtml: Harms that spread unchecked because safeguards or pauses were stripped away. It is the opposite of friction added on purpose to slow harm. It appears when nothing slows fast automated steps and nothing asks people to confirm irreversible actions.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.

entries.title: Coercive consent
entries.bodyHtml:
“Agreement” obtained through defaults, asymmetry, or threats of exclusion — consent produced by lack of viable refusal. It is the opposite of consent depth.

It is manufactured by contracts of adhesion and refusability failures, and laundered by dropout-as-legitimation.
entries.scope: I. Friction & flow. Where a system slows, pauses, or asks for confirmation before it acts, and who carries the cost of that friction.
operationalTests: Consent is scored by the viability of refusal, not the presence of an “I agree” click.
A default that excludes on refusal is flagged as coercive regardless of wording.
entries.genealogy: Defines consent by the real option to refuse, not by the signature.

categories.heading: J. Decision states & edges
categories.descriptionHtml: Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Decision edge
entries.bodyHtml: The precise moment when a choice shifts from reversible to consequential. Making it visible allows confirmation steps and clearer consent at that moment, and an automatic halt when risk spikes.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Decision artifact
entries.bodyHtml:
One decision's output, in a form that can be traced to its owner and challenged. It records the outcome, the reason, the time, and the accountable owner.

Decision artifacts anchor traceable ownership and make contestability measurable.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Decision object
entries.bodyHtml:
A versioned record of the rules, inputs, thresholds, and authority behind an operational decision. It names an owner and states whether the decision can be appealed or reversed, and on what clock. A decision that affects someone's access, status, or rights must be backed by an active decision object.

For example, the decision object for an eligibility rule might name Risk Operations as owner and cite the policy section that delegates the decision. It lists two inputs, verified income and months employed, and three possible outputs: approved, denied, or pending review. It allows reversal by human override under a reversal SLA, and appeal under a binding clock.

The object turns “the system decided” into “this record decided, and this role owns it.” Once it exists, there is something to appeal and someone who has to answer.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Binding clock
entries.bodyHtml:
An enforceable timer on an institution's obligations once a decision is pending or contested. It keeps running regardless of workload, staffing, or queue length, and pauses only under conditions declared in advance.

For example, a clock might start when a decision enters pending review. It can pause only for an agreed extension or a documented outside dependency, and only with an ombuds officer's approval on a public log. When it runs out, the case goes to human review and the person gets interim access. The person can see the clock.

Without a binding clock, delay works as power, silence is read as consent, and “we’re reviewing” has no end. With one, the institution pays for the waiting.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Reversal SLA
entries.bodyHtml:
A commitment that states the maximum time, the authority, and the procedure for undoing or correcting a decision once it is contested or found wrong. Reversal performance is a reliability measure, not an exception process.

For example, a contract clause might require the provider to start human review within 24 hours of a valid reversal request, and to reverse or affirm the decision within 5 business days. If it misses either deadline, the person's access is restored in the interim and the provider owes service credits. Escalation runs from the operations lead to the risk director to an independent reviewer.

A decision object records what was decided and who owns it. A binding clock limits how long a decision can stay pending. A reversal SLA limits how long a wrong decision can stand. Together they turn “you can appeal” into “an appeal changes what the institution owes.”
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Non-decision
entries.bodyHtml:
A stable administrative disposition where a system withholds a contestable outcome (“pending,” “in review”) while consequences accrue.

Non-decisions stretch moral latency and erode contestability by keeping people in limbo.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Unearned closure
entries.bodyHtml:
The system marks something resolved without repairing the underlying harm; the residual cost remains with the person.

Unearned closure converts unresolved obligations into status changes and often hides behind attrition-as-resolution or closure-code regimes.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Stable clock
entries.bodyHtml:
A non-resettable timeline for a case; the system cannot restart time via re-ticketing, re-verification, or channel switching.

Stable clocks enforce bounded duration and keep timelines legible.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Utility window
entries.bodyHtml:
The time span during which relief can still prevent the relevant harm.

Designing for a clear utility window keeps time-to-restore accountable.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Futility threshold
entries.bodyHtml:
The point where time-on-task or repetition becomes so costly that valid claimants predictably abandon pursuit.

Systems that hit the futility threshold signal punitive friction and low contestability.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Constructive denial
entries.bodyHtml:
A legal state where delay is treated as refusal, because the delay has made relief useless or pursuing it futile.

The trigger is utility expiry: relief that arrives after the window in which it could still help. Constructive denial forces accountable remedies rather than letting the delay stand as an administrative outcome.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Critical action
entries.bodyHtml: Any system action that meaningfully alters a person’s status, access, or trajectory. Critical actions require dignity friction.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Irreversible boundary
entries.bodyHtml: A threshold the system cannot automatically undo — account closures, public releases, or data publication. Crossing it demands stronger ways to challenge the decision, audited explanations, and an explicit plan for restoring people.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Ethical interrupts
entries.bodyHtml:
Automatic system-level halts triggered by anomalies, harm indicators, or policy boundary breaches. Ethical interrupts operationalize stoppability by turning warning signals into enforceable pauses.

They must include clear ownership, audit trails, and restart criteria so pauses protect people without becoming arbitrary lockouts.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
examples: A model-serving pipeline halts promotion when subgroup harm metrics breach policy limits and requires cross-functional signoff before restart.

entries.title: Actionability threshold
entries.bodyHtml: The level of confidence, authorization, and oversight required before information becomes action. Raising the actionability threshold protects against low-signal decisions and clarifies design authority.
examples: A fraud alert triggers action only after confidence and authorization checks.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Normative uncertainty
entries.bodyHtml: Situations where it is unclear what the “right” action is, requiring caution, clarification, or human judgment rather than confident automation. It often calls for an automatic halt and a higher bar of confidence and authorization before acting.
examples: When guidance conflicts, the system pauses and requests human judgment.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.

entries.title: Harm receipt
entries.bodyHtml: A claimant-facing artifact documenting what happened, what the system believes, and what it will do next, by when. Harm receipts make decision artifacts legible to affected people.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: Receipts are issued automatically for defined incident classes and include a named owner and a clock.
Receipts capture what happened, the system’s belief, and the next steps with timelines.

entries.title: Access cliff
entries.bodyHtml: A threshold where small variance causes catastrophic loss of service, such as lockout, termination, or loss of benefits. Access cliffs are mitigated with soft edges and gradual ramps.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: An access cliff inventory exists with mandated soft edges or gradual ramps.
Policies prohibit catastrophic loss from minor variance without a graduated path.

entries.title: Expansion decision
entries.bodyHtml:
A separate authorization decision taken when an existing delegation is widened in scope, population, autonomy, or consequence. It carries its own evidence, its own correction capacity check, and its own dependence review, and it is recorded as a transition on the grant.

It matters because expansion is normally treated as the reward for success rather than as a new delegation. Requiring the decision is the direct block on the automation ratchet, and it keeps an authority grant readable against what the system now does.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: Widening a delegation cannot be shipped without an expansion record naming its evidence.
The record includes a correction capacity check and a dependence review, not only a risk note.
Expansion transitions are visible in the grant's state history.
entries.genealogy: Turns Law XI into a decision state, so that growth in delegated authority has the same ceremony as its creation.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An expansion record with evidence, correction capacity check, and dependence review.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An expansion deferred because correction capacity had not grown with the proposed scope.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of scope increases accompanied by an expansion record.
minimumEvidence.threshold: Target 100%; gaps are reconciled as authority drift.

entries.title: Non-finality
entries.bodyHtml:
The property that a decisive action does not close its own categories, evidence, or jurisdiction against revision. A system with non-finality can act now and be corrected later; a system whose decisions become final by default converts each exercise of power into an entitlement. Appeal is its instrument at the level of outcomes, and meta-contestability extends it to the rules of challenge themselves. Non-finality is not indecision: the system acts now. A case left undecided is pendingness, which is a harm in its own right.

It matters because finality is how power consolidates quietly: an initial judgment that cannot be reopened becomes precedent for the next, and the category that produced the judgment becomes harder to question than the judgment itself. The rights tradition names the interruption — appeal interrupts the conversion of decision into finality — and Law XII bars consuming the capacity that keeps it possible.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: A decided outcome can be reopened on stated grounds without extraordinary procedure.
Categories and evidentiary rules stay revisable after decisions were made under them.
The institution's jurisdiction itself can be challenged, not only its outcomes.
entries.genealogy: Completes the framework's five concerns — jurisdiction, representation, residual custody, corrigibility, and the property that keeps all four revisable.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A reopen register: decided outcomes with the grounds and clock on which each can be reopened.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A decision reopened on stated grounds, with the category or rule it questioned still changeable.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential decision classes with a stated reopen route and clock.

entries.title: Decision surface
entries.bodyHtml:
The part of a system where decisions become visible, addressable, and contestable. Many systems minimize the decision surface to avoid accountability.

It is the territory shaped by the interaction surface, populated by decision objects, and opened or closed by contestability.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: Every consequential decision exposes a surface that can be addressed.
A shrinking decision surface is treated as a governance regression.
entries.genealogy: Makes the addressability of decisions a designed, auditable property.

entries.title: Object formation
entries.bodyHtml:
The process by which a complaint, harm, or request becomes a formal case: it is assigned an identifier, a category, an owner, a standard of review, and a clock. Systems often block accountability by preventing object formation (“nothing exists to appeal”).

It is the gate that a harm receipt must pass to become a decision object.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: Every received harm forms an object with id, owner, standard, and clock.
Failure to form an object is an auditable failure, not a filing quirk.
entries.genealogy: Makes the birth of a decision object a governed event rather than an assumption.

entries.title: Pending / pendingness
entries.bodyHtml:
A state in which nothing is decided and no one is obliged to decide. It is often presented as neutral, but it allocates outcomes: the party that can wait longer wins. Pendingness becomes harm when it has no clock, no owner, or no forced next step.

It is not non-finality. Non-finality means a decision has been made and stays open to revision. Pendingness means no decision has been made, so there is nothing to revise or appeal. It persists through delay as power wherever no binding clock runs.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: Every pending state carries a clock and an owner by default.
Indefinite pending without obligation is flagged as harm, not neutrality.
entries.genealogy: Reveals the neutral-sounding “pending” as an allocator of outcomes.

entries.title: Settlement
entries.bodyHtml:
The moment a claim becomes resolved in a way that changes the underlying state — approved, denied with appeal rights, remediated, reversed, paid, restored, or otherwise closed with consequences. Settlement is not closure in the CRM; it is resolution that binds.

It is the outcome that bindingness makes possible and that closure-code regimes often fake.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: A settled claim changes underlying state, not only its ticket status.
Settlement is distinguished from closure that binds nothing.
entries.genealogy: Reserves “settled” for resolution that binds the institution.

entries.title: Non-settlement / nonsettlement
entries.bodyHtml:
An institutional mode where claims are acknowledged and processed indefinitely without producing a binding resolution. The system offers intake, updates, and politeness while keeping obligation optional.

It is the operational home of attrition-as-resolution and unearned closure.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: A claim is scored by whether it reached binding resolution, not by how long it was processed.
Institutions distinguish activity on a claim from settlement of it.
entries.genealogy: Names the indefinite-processing mode that pretends to be adjudication.

entries.title: Clock-start / clock mismatch
entries.bodyHtml:
Clock-start: the moment a system becomes time-bound — deadlines begin, obligations attach, escalation becomes meaningful. Clock mismatch: when institutional execution is fast (instant flags, freezes, denials) but redress is slow (weeks to months of human review), making errors durable and contestation scarce.

It is the temporal form of binding clocks versus reversal SLAs.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: Every decision has a defined clock-start, not an open-ended one.
Execution and redress latency are compared; a large gap is flagged as a defect.
entries.genealogy: Makes the asymmetry between action speed and correction speed explicit.

entries.title: Slow redress / fast execution
entries.bodyHtml:
A governance asymmetry where harmful state changes are immediate but appeals are delayed, discretionary, and exhausting. The gap lets an institution coerce without deciding to: the harm lands at once, and the remedy arrives late or not at all.

It is degradation-restoration asymmetry in its temporal form, and what time-to-restore is measured against.
