entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: Harm and remedy latencies are measured separately and compared.
A fast-execution/slow-redress gap is treated as a coercion indicator, not a cost tradeoff.
entries.genealogy: Isolates the speed asymmetry that makes harm cheap and correction expensive.

entries.title: Irreversibility
entries.bodyHtml:
A state where reversal is practically unavailable (too slow, too expensive, too discretionary) even if it is theoretically possible. Irreversibility is often produced by missing clocks, missing authority, or asymmetric evidence demands.

It is the condition that irreversibility indices measure and that irreversible boundaries are drawn to prevent.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: A state is classified as irreversible when reversal is practically unavailable, not only theoretically impossible.
The mechanism producing irreversibility (missing clock, authority, or evidence) is named.
entries.genealogy: Distinguishes practical irreversibility from theoretical possibility.

entries.title: Backstop
entries.bodyHtml:
A guaranteed fallback mechanism that triggers when the main process fails — timeouts, automatic approvals, emergency restoration, or external review. Backstops prevent the silent failure of the primary path.

They are the implementation of safe pause and the guarantee behind time-to-halt.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: Every critical path has a fallback that triggers automatically on failure.
A backstop is tested end to end, not specified in a runbook.
entries.genealogy: Makes graceful failure a designed guarantee rather than an aspiration.

entries.title: Rollback
entries.bodyHtml:
A designed ability to revert the system to a prior safe state — restoring access, undoing propagation, correcting records — ideally with minimal friction. Rollback is the technical face of reversibility.

It is bounded by time-to-restore and depends on restoration completeness.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: A prior safe state is reachable without disproportionate friction.
Rollback covers downstream propagation, not only the original record.
entries.genealogy: Turns reversal from a hope into an engineered operation.

entries.title: Auto-close / auto-renew / auto-share
entries.bodyHtml:
Default state transitions that happen without active consent — closing claims, renewing contracts, expanding data use — often presented as convenience while functioning as governance by inertia. They are defaults as governance in action.

Each silent transition is a site where meaningful control is quietly surrendered.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: No consequential state transition happens without active, recent consent.
An auto-transition is audited for who benefited and who lost control.
entries.genealogy: Names the inertia defaults that convert convenience into coercion.

entries.title: Silence defaults to approval
entries.bodyHtml:
A rule under which an unanswered application, appeal, or prior-authorization request resolves in the applicant's favor when the institution misses a stated clock. Law VIII already holds that silence past the clock is a governance failure rather than a pending state; this names the state the request enters instead.

The rule reverses the default. While an institution misses its clock at no cost, delay is an externality carried by the person waiting and latency stays free to the party that caused it. Putting the outcome on the institution's side of the ledger at a fixed hour is what makes the clock binding.

Applies beside binding clock, reversal SLA, and slow redress, fast execution.
entries.scope: J. Decision states & edges. Where and how decisions flip from reversible to permanent.
operationalTests: A stated clock names the state a request enters when it expires, not only that the institution has failed.
The clock runs in units a person can read and expires on a date the institution can see coming.
Where the applicant loses more than the institution by a wrong outcome, the default names an escalation rather than a grant.

categories.heading: K. Patterns & anti-patterns
categories.descriptionHtml: Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.

entries.title: Heroism-dependent systems
entries.bodyHtml:
Systems that rely on extraordinary effort, unpaid care, or silent sacrifice to function. The effort hides a system that is hard to stop and does heavy harm when it fails.

The heroism is a fallback nobody wrote down, which is normalized dependence in its human form. Counting that effort into dependency state makes it a budget item rather than a virtue.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.

entries.title: Empathy surrogacy
entries.bodyHtml: Simulated warmth — chatbots, scripted apologies, tone guidelines — used to mask structural harm or delay fixes. Empathy surrogacy diverts attention from repair and weakens contestability by substituting sentiment for remedy.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.

entries.title: Error cascades
entries.bodyHtml:
Small automated mistakes that amplify across the system through retries, shared dependencies, or blind handoffs. Error cascades are rarely one bug: they are chain reactions in tightly coupled workflows.

Containment depends on ethical interrupts, clear rollback boundaries, and fairness and safety measures that trigger action before harms compound.
examples: A flawed fraud rule mislabels transactions, which triggers automatic account locks, support backlog spikes, and delayed rent payments.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.

entries.title: Invisible fallbacks
entries.bodyHtml: Hidden behaviors that appear under stress — shadow queues, silent throttling, or undocumented overrides. They hide who can stop, reverse, or repair harm. They should be brought into the open as prepared routes to reverse decisions and rehearsed during scheduled maintenance.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.

entries.title: Dead-user zones
entries.bodyHtml: Places where people affected by decisions cannot contest, appeal, or exit — opaque rankings, automated bans, or unmoderated queues. Closing them requires giving people more room to act and raising the share of appeals that succeed.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.

entries.title: Moral lock-in
entries.bodyHtml:
When harmful defaults become entrenched through dependencies, network effects, or contracts that block reform. It is prevented by deciding whether the system should act at all before it starts, by keeping its decisions open to challenge, and by checking continuously for drift from what it was authorized to do.

Lock-in usually begins as normalized dependence: reliance nobody records until reform requires reversing it. Tracking dependency state turns lock-in from a late discovery into a measurement taken early.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.

entries.title: Withdrawal rehearsal
entries.bodyHtml:
A scheduled exercise in which a system is stood down, in whole or in a bounded slice, and the fallback carries real work for a stated period. The rehearsal produces timings, failures, and a list of what did not work.

It matters because untested withdrawal is a claim rather than a capacity. Rehearsal is the evidence that separates operational reversibility from a diagram, and it is how preserved capacity is kept alive rather than merely listed.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: Rehearsals are scheduled on a cadence and are not canceled for load.
The rehearsal uses production volume for a bounded slice, not a synthetic replay.
Findings become funded work items with owners, not observations in a report.
entries.genealogy: The practice that produces evidence for Laws VI and XII, adapted from disaster recovery exercises to the withdrawal of a depended-upon system.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A rehearsal plan and report with scope, duration, timings, and findings.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A rehearsal completed at production volume with the fallback carrying the work.
minimumEvidence.metric: Interval since last rehearsal, and share of findings closed before the next one.

entries.title: Polite coercion
entries.bodyHtml:
Coercion delivered through soothing language and “helpful” workflows that make refusal costly or stigmatized. Polite coercion is power that avoids looking like power.

It pairs with tone policing and launders coercive consent through legitimacy laundering.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: A workflow is scored by the real cost of refusal, not by its tone.
Soothing language that raises refusal cost is flagged as coercion.
entries.genealogy: Makes the soothing register of coercion visible as coercion.

entries.title: Documentation loop / resubmission loop
entries.bodyHtml:
A repeating pattern where the system continually requests more evidence or re-uploads without moving toward a binding decision. Often used to shift labor onto claimants and to manufacture dropout.

It is burden transfer with a smile, and a feeder of attrition-as-resolution.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: Each repeated request moves the claim closer to a binding decision.
A request that does not advance the decision is flagged as a loop, not progress.
entries.genealogy: Makes the resubmission loop legible as delay machinery.

entries.title: Precision demands
entries.bodyHtml:
Requests for ever-greater specificity that function less as truth-seeking and more as denial hooks — ways to keep a case non-objectified or non-decidable. Precision demands are a technique of delay.

They prevent object formation and are the mirror of documentation loops.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: A specificity request is scored by whether it advances or stalls the decision.
A demand that cannot be met is flagged as a denial hook, not due diligence.
entries.genealogy: Separates genuine evidentiary need from precision used as a stall.

entries.title: Procedural alibi
entries.bodyHtml:
A record of “process” used to defend outcomes (“we followed procedure”) even when the procedure cannot bind the institution to remedy. The alibi is the trace of activity, not accountability.

It is the paper form of procedural force without power, and the close cousin of paper compliance.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: Procedure is scored by whether it can bind the institution, not by whether it was followed.
A “we followed procedure” defense is tested against remedy, not against the process log.
entries.genealogy: Exposes procedure-as-alibi where activity substitutes for remedy.

entries.title: Tone policing (as governance technology)
entries.bodyHtml:
The use of “appropriate tone” requirements to control access to remedy — penalizing anger, urgency, neurodivergent communication, or exhaustion. Tone policing converts distress into disqualification.

It is the affective edge of polite coercion, and it defeats affect-invariance.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: Access to remedy does not depend on the claimant’s tone or composure.
A distress signal is treated as information, not as a disqualifier.
entries.genealogy: Makes the affective gate on remedy visible as a governance mechanism.

entries.title: Dropout-as-legitimation
entries.bodyHtml:
When systems treat nonresponse, fatigue, or disappearance as consent or closure (“case closed — no reply”), laundering coercion into “resolved.” Dropout becomes the mechanism that protects the institution.

It is attrition-as-resolution wearing the face of user inaction, producing unearned closure.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: Nonresponse is never treated as consent or as a decision.
Dropout is investigated as a possible coercion outcome, not logged as “resolved.”
entries.genealogy: Reads silence as an outcome the system manufactured, not as user choice.

entries.title: Churn (as closure mechanism)
entries.bodyHtml:
The engineered cycling of people through forms, queues, and handoffs until they give up, miss a deadline, or become “inactive,” allowing the system to close without settlement. Churn is manufactured attrition.

It is the machinery behind dropout-as-legitimation and a producer of attrition-as-resolution.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: Handoff counts are audited as a closure mechanism, not as service.
A case that closes from inactivity is reopened on the merits, not closed silently.
entries.genealogy: Names the deliberate cycling that converts process friction into closure.

entries.title: Paper compliance / checkbox governance
entries.bodyHtml:
Compliance regimes focused on producing documentation of doing the right thing rather than mechanisms that can prevent harm or force remedy. The paperwork stands in for power.

It is the institutional form of procedural alibi, and the failure mode behind compliance collapse.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: Compliance is scored by a mechanism’s effect on harm, not by its documentation.
A checklist without a binding effect is flagged as paper, not compliance.
entries.genealogy: Distinguishes documentary compliance from enforceable compliance.

entries.title: Transparency theater
entries.bodyHtml:
Disclosures that do not increase contestability — more text, more dashboards, more “explanations” — without deadlines, authority, or reversal paths. Visibility substitutes for enforceability.

It is the disclosure form of paper compliance and the complement of explainability decoy.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: A disclosure is scored by whether it increases contestability, not by its volume.
Visibility without a reversal path is flagged as theater, not transparency.
entries.genealogy: Exposes visibility as a substitute for the enforceability it should enable.

entries.title: Explainability decoy
entries.bodyHtml:
A focus on explaining model decisions that distracts from the harder question: can the decision be contested, reversed, and time-bounded? The decoy offers epistemics where governance is needed.

It redirects attention from explainability for accountability toward explanation for its own sake.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: An explanation is scored by whether it enables contestation and reversal.
Explainability effort is measured against its effect on remedy, not its detail.
entries.genealogy: Names the substitution of explanation for enforceable accountability.

entries.title: Human-in-the-loop (as legitimacy artifact)
entries.bodyHtml:
A human reviewer inserted to create legitimacy while lacking binding authority, deadlines, or meaningful discretion. The loop becomes a comfort signal, not a power shift.

It is the person-shaped form of rubber-stamp review, distinguished from real binding authority.
entries.scope: K. System patterns & anti-patterns. Recurring structures institutions build, most of them ways that process, tone, or disclosure stands in for remedy.
operationalTests: A human reviewer’s authority and deadlines are specified, not assumed.
A loop that cannot change state is flagged as a legitimacy artifact.
entries.genealogy: Makes the human-in-the-loop visible as a legitimacy device when it lacks power.

categories.heading: L. Open research areas
categories.descriptionHtml: Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Structural gentleness coefficients
entries.bodyHtml: Measures of how much ordinary human variance an infrastructure tolerates before it fails someone: error tolerance, recovery time, and soft edges. Higher coefficients are expected to track lower failure load and safer degradation.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Burden elasticity
entries.bodyHtml: How effort and risk move between parties when conditions change, and whether they move back afterward. Mapping burden elasticity alongside the burden gradient shows whether a crisis will land on the people with the least power to refuse it.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Care redundancy
entries.bodyHtml: Overlapping routes through people, automated checks, and policy guarantees, so that when one safeguard fails another still catches the person. With controlled degradation, it keeps the harm done by any one failure low.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Meta-contestability
entries.bodyHtml: Mechanisms that let people challenge the rules of challenge as well as its outcomes: who may appeal, what evidence counts, and who sits on review panels. Meta-contestability keeps contestability from ossifying.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: User-state modeling for harm prevention
entries.bodyHtml: Inferring user states such as fatigue, distress, or inattention to slow the pace, add protective friction, or route to a person before harm compounds. The models must respect anticipatory consent and must not create new burden transfers. And the models read the machine's trail — non-attributable aggregates of error counts and queue depth — not the person: gaze tracking, keystroke dynamics, and attention scoring are operator instrumentation, and a protective signal that watches the operator becomes a quota under incentive pressure.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Design for ethical latency
entries.bodyHtml: Designing for the unavoidable delay between an action and its review: staging risky steps, slowing fast automated steps, or keeping baseline commitments to people in place until the fuller review is done.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Adaptive refusal pathways
entries.bodyHtml: Flows that reroute a task when someone pauses or declines, keeping the case context and imposing no penalty. They let a person decline more than once without losing their place, and they keep the system usable when people refuse. See refusal budget and refusal tolerance.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Aftercare automation
entries.bodyHtml: Automated follow-up after an incident that checks on the people affected, schedules remedies, and prompts a named person to close the case. Done well, it reduces harm not yet repaired without adding work for the people involved.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Alignment dividend
entries.bodyHtml: The measurable gains in trust, retention, and safety when a system serves the people it acts on as intended. Tracking the dividend is the budget argument for sustained funding of halt, reversal, and appeal measures and maintenance metabolism.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Ambiguity budgets
entries.bodyHtml: Explicit allowances for uncertainty that hold back automation or strict enforcement until there is enough context. The budget reserves time, human review, or maintenance windows for the cases that need them.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Anticipatory consent
entries.bodyHtml: Consent models that preview future data uses and let people pre-approve, defer, or block them. Anticipatory consent supports rights of exit and counters precision laundering of unclear terms.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Care floor guarantees
entries.bodyHtml: Baseline commitments a service keeps during outages or crises: live support, data export, or safe defaults. Care floors protect users while graceful degradation is active.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Compassion telemetry
entries.bodyHtml: Signals about how people are treated in an interaction: response tone, wait times during distress, and whether follow-up happened. They sit beside technical metrics and protect compassion bandwidth.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Conflict observability
entries.bodyHtml: Logging that records a conflict between values when it happens, for example when fairness and safety measures are traded against throughput or appeals spike. The record lets the conflict be reviewed before it escalates and lets correction start sooner.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Counter-abuse guardrails
entries.bodyHtml: Limits that stop tools from being repurposed for harassment, exploitation, or coercion: rate limits, anomaly detection, and override paths tuned for abuse cases.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Crisis rehearsal loops
entries.bodyHtml: Regular drills that test how a system responds to harm, as well as whether it stays up. They exercise the automatic halts, check the baseline commitments kept during outages, and record findings in the repair log.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Data dignity budgets
entries.bodyHtml: Caps on what data is collected and how it is used, set by context and purpose rather than by what a consent checkbox legally allows. They fit with letting people approve, defer, or block future uses in advance, and guard against taking data without return.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Downstream equity buffers
entries.bodyHtml: Design slack that absorbs variance so marginalized groups do not pay first or most when errors occur. Buffers include staggered rollouts, rollback lanes, and targeted support funds.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Ethical load testing
entries.bodyHtml: Exercises that probe how a system behaves when its safeguards are under stress, such as simulated harassment, mass appeals, or outages, to check that ethical circuit breakers trip and care floors hold.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Exhaustion triggers
entries.bodyHtml: Signals that detect operator or user fatigue, such as error streaks, long queues, and late-night decisions, and automatically slow, pause, or hand off a flow before mistakes multiply. The triggers protect compassion bandwidth.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Friction budgets
entries.bodyHtml: A planned allocation of protective and dignity friction across a workflow, set step by step according to risk, instead of removing friction wherever it slows things down.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Harm amnesty windows
entries.bodyHtml: Time-boxed periods where people can report or reverse harmful actions without penalty, encouraging disclosure and faster repair. Amnesty windows often follow rehearsal loops or incidents.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Heat maps of refusal
entries.bodyHtml: Maps of where people opt out, churn, or appeal, which show early where refusal is being made costly. They are used to tune refusal budgets and redesign interaction surfaces.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Incident memory chains
entries.bodyHtml: Linked records that attach the findings from past incidents to the workflows most like them, so the next team sees them before repeating the failure. Memory chains inform ethical load tests and prevent moral lock-in on bad patterns.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Moral dry runs
entries.bodyHtml: Pre-launch walkthroughs that play out the hard cases a design will meet, such as conflicting obligations or a wrong decision nobody can reverse, before it reaches the public. Dry runs test circuit breakers, rollback lanes, and documentation.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Refusal-aware routing
entries.bodyHtml: Routing logic that knows who can decline a task and makes sure a refusal is honored without retaliation or a silent penalty. It preserves refusal budgets so that declining stays a real option.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Relief invariants
entries.bodyHtml: Guarantees that relief takes the same predictable effort and support whichever path a person comes in by. Relief invariants are tested in crisis rehearsals and anchored by care floors.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Repair quorums
entries.bodyHtml: Minimum participation rules for authorizing fixes so impacted communities have a seat in deciding remedies. Repair quorums counter accountability diffusion and legitimize restitution.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

entries.title: Rest cycle enforcement
entries.bodyHtml: Built-in mechanisms that enforce rest and recovery — rotation policies, cooldown timers, enforced downtime — so fatigue does not translate into harm. It protects the routine upkeep a service needs and the emotional labor people can sustain.
entries.scope: L. Future concepts / research areas. Open research threads: terms in use that do not yet carry operational tests or a minimum evidence standard.

categories.heading: M. Foundational principles
categories.descriptionHtml: The principles the method's laws and standards rest on.

entries.title: The conservancy principle
entries.bodyHtml: Designers hold the people a system affects and the resources it draws on in trust, and must leave systems safer and easier to repair than they found them. It gives priority to repair, to keeping the system stoppable, and to paying down harm not yet repaired.
entries.scope: M. Foundational Ethotechnic principles. The principles the method's laws and standards rest on.

entries.title: The burden inversion rule
entries.bodyHtml: When harm occurs, the system shoulders effort before the person harmed does. Burden inversion lowers the user burden ratio and demands rapid restoration.
entries.scope: M. Foundational Ethotechnic principles. The principles the method's laws and standards rest on.

entries.title: The stop-before-explain rule
entries.bodyHtml: Halt harmful behavior first, then justify or refine it. The automatic stop comes before any explanation, so the harm can still be undone.
entries.scope: M. Foundational Ethotechnic principles. The principles the method's laws and standards rest on.

entries.title: The maintenance doctrine
entries.bodyHtml:
A system stays safe to rely on only while it is maintained: routine upkeep that is funded, scheduled pauses for inspection and repair, and repair records people can read. Maintenance is a standing obligation, not a cleanup phase.

The doctrine requires institutions to budget for prevention, rehearsal, and repair before incidents force emergency tradeoffs.
entries.scope: M. Foundational Ethotechnic principles. The principles the method's laws and standards rest on.
examples: A product roadmap reserves recurring capacity for incident rehearsal and remediation work, protected from feature-priority overrides.

entries.title: The principle of low-failure-load design
entries.bodyHtml: Design so that when failures occur, human impact is contained. It is the reason for controlled degradation, baseline commitments kept during outages, and a low share of actions that cannot be undone.
entries.scope: M. Foundational Ethotechnic principles. The principles the method's laws and standards rest on.

entries.title: The reversibility mandate
entries.bodyHtml:
Any action that changes a person's status, access, or trajectory must be undoable, or come with prepared routes to reverse it that work in real operating conditions.

If reversal is impossible, systems should add explicit guardrails, higher review thresholds, and public ownership of residual risk.
examples: A benefits eligibility model deployment is blocked unless the team demonstrates a tested rollback path and a 24-hour restoration plan.
entries.scope: M. Foundational Ethotechnic principles. The principles the method's laws and standards rest on.

entries.title: Policy as state
entries.bodyHtml:
The rule that policy is a state of the running system rather than an input consumed at deployment. A policy record has a version, assumptions, an expiry, and a current status that other objects can read and react to.

It matters because policy held as a document cannot take part in control. Only policy held as state lets an assumption going stale change an authority grant without anyone remembering to look.
entries.scope: M. Foundational Ethotechnic principles. The principles the method's laws and standards rest on.
operationalTests: Policy status is queryable at runtime by the component that enforces authorization.
A policy change produces a state transition somewhere, or the change is recorded as non-binding.
No enforcement path depends on a human reading a policy document at the right moment.
entries.genealogy: States the second half of Law III as a design principle: policy is state, not input.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A runtime policy status endpoint or table that authorization checks read.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An authorization refused because the policy backing it was in a lapsed status.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of enforceable policies with a machine-readable current status.

entries.title: Meaningful control
entries.bodyHtml:
The conditions under which a human counts as part of a control system. They can see the problem, hold authority to prevent or alter the action, have time to act, have a defined path when they disagree, and face incentives that permit disagreement. Anything less is presence, not control.

It matters because oversight is easy to claim and hard to evidence. Meaningful control is tested through an intervention specification, and its absence is what turns review into rubber-stamp review.
entries.scope: M. Foundational Ethotechnic principles. The principles the method's laws and standards rest on.
operationalTests: Reviewers can name the state they can change and the time budget they have to change it.
Disagreement has a defined route that does not depend on personal risk appetite.
Approval rates and reversal rates are both reported, not approval rates alone.
entries.genealogy: States Law IX as a principle a deployment either satisfies or does not, replacing the claim that a human is involved.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An oversight assessment answering the Law IX question set for each review point.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A reviewer halting or altering an action, with the trajectory change visible in logs.
minimumEvidence.metric: Reviewer-initiated state changes per thousand reviews, alongside median review time.

entries.title: The non-conversion principle
entries.bodyHtml:
The rule that a fact about a system does not become a fact about its authority on its own. Capability, elapsed time without observed failure, and successful operation are evidence that a grant might be justified; none of them is a grant. Authority changes only through an explicit, recorded state transition, with the motivating fact attached as its basis. Confidence is a further instance: a high posterior about a person is evidence for a decision, never the authorization to act on them.

It matters because the conversions it refuses are the ones institutions make by default: a tool is reachable so it is used, a system has been quiet so it stays, a pilot went well so the rollout is not a decision. Laws I, II, and XI are the instances that matter most for delegated intelligence, and each is enforced by holding capability, evidence, and authority in different objects rather than by a rule of conduct. The authority grant and its state history are where a permitted conversion is written down.
entries.scope: M. Foundational Ethotechnic principles. The principles the method's laws and standards rest on.
operationalTests: Capability records and authority records are held in separate objects, and the first cannot write to the second.
Every widening or renewal of a grant appears as a recorded transition with a stated basis.
A capability that is reachable but not granted is refused, and the refusal is checkable by a harness.
entries.genealogy: Names the shape shared by Laws I, II, and XI, and argued for in the theory essay on what does not convert.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A grant whose state history shows each expansion and renewal as a transition with a recorded basis.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A reachable capability refused at execution because no grant covers it.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of grant widenings that occurred as recorded transitions rather than being discovered after the fact.

entries.title: Post-optimization rigor
entries.bodyHtml:
The engineering posture for the point where optimization runs out. Optimizing a metric or reward function invites Goodhart drift, leaves out what the metric cannot see, and produces residual complexity.

Post-optimization rigor does not try to fix model incompleteness by adding more parameters or objective terms. It builds the institution around the model instead: independent review, measurement of uncounted absorption, corrective standing for affected parties, and revocable authority grants.
entries.scope: M. Foundational Ethotechnic principles. The principles the method's laws and standards rest on.
operationalTests: The deployment pairs every optimized model with an independent correction and contestation infrastructure.
Performance audits track externalized friction and absorption rather than relying solely on internal loss functions or proxy metrics.
entries.genealogy: Moves the work from improving the model to building the institution around it.

entries.title: Human non-substitutability
entries.bodyHtml:
The ground rule that a model of a person is not the person: no representation, however accurate, acquires automatic authority to extinguish the represented person's standing against it. A system may infer, classify, predict, and recommend, but the person remains the party who carries the consequences and whose contestation the system must answer.

It matters because the framework's treatment of corrective standing rests on it. Standing is inalienable, not generous: if the subject of a decision could be replaced by a sufficiently detailed model of themselves, contestation would be a quality-control step a good enough model could close. Accuracy is evidence for a decision; it is never the decision, and it never substitutes for the person.
entries.scope: M. Foundational Ethotechnic principles. The principles the method's laws and standards rest on.
operationalTests: A system acting on an inference about a person can name what that person's challenge would do to the action.
Model accuracy is never cited as a reason a person's contestation is unnecessary.
The subject of a decision is identified separately from the user of the system.
entries.genealogy: The ground rule under Law VII, argued for in the theory of what a model of a person is and is not.

references.label: The model of a person is not the person

minimumEvidence.artifact: A decision record that names the person it acts on and the route by which that person can contest it.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A challenge by the represented person that reaches the inference that justified the action.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of consequential decisions where the represented person's contestation route is recorded.

entries.title: Safe incompleteness
entries.bodyHtml:
The design stance that a system should improve its representation of people and preserve their contestation at the same time, because the two capacities compound rather than substitute for each other. The error it opposes is closure without remainder: treating the model boundary as the boundary of relevance, so that every mismatch between the model and the person reads as user error, anomalous input, or noise.

It matters because a system that is incomplete and contestable is safer than one that is complete and final. The complete one has nowhere for its errors to arrive; the incomplete one constitutionalizes the failure path instead of optimizing it away, and the challenge route is the mechanism by which the representation's errors are discovered at all.
entries.scope: M. Foundational Ethotechnic principles. The principles the method's laws and standards rest on.
operationalTests: Better model performance is paired with preserved or widened contestation routes, not narrowed ones.
The system can state what its representation does not cover.
A mismatch between the model and the person can enter the system as an event with state-changing force.
entries.genealogy: The design consequence of closure without remainder: incompleteness is permanent, so contestability is the safety mechanism.

references.label: The model of a person is not the person

minimumEvidence.artifact: A stated coverage boundary: what the model represents, what it does not, and where challenges arrive.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A representation improvement shipped without narrowing any contestation route.
minimumEvidence.metric: Contestation route reach after each representation upgrade, compared with before.

entries.title: Anti-conversion rights
entries.bodyHtml:
The reading of rights as barriers that stop one kind of power turning into another without authorization. Privacy interrupts the conversion of knowledge into action. Due process interrupts the conversion of institutional position into outcome. Consent rules interrupt the conversion of access into authority. Appeal interrupts the conversion of decision into finality. Separation of powers interrupts the conversion of execution into evaluation.

It matters because it states what rights are for in Ethotechnic terms: not protections added around power, but the mechanisms that keep a capability from becoming an authorization. The non-conversion principle is the general form; the rights are its specific, historically won instances.
entries.scope: M. Foundational Ethotechnic principles. The principles the method's laws and standards rest on.
operationalTests: Each enumerated right on a deployment can be named as the conversion it interrupts.
A capability that a right blocks is recorded as unavailable, not as pending approval.
Removing a right would widen some authority surface, and that widening is named.
entries.genealogy: Extends the non-conversion principle from capability to the constitutional instruments that enforce it.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A rights-to-conversions map for the deployment: each right, and the capability it keeps from becoming authority.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An inference blocked from producing action because the right in question does not permit the conversion.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of enumerated rights with a named conversion they interrupt.

entries.title: The excluded case
entries.bodyHtml:
The principle that a case a representation leaves out may be evidence about the category, not merely noise around it. It is the epistemological ground of institutional fallibilism. A complaint can be knowledge. Repeated exception handling can reveal more about a system than its official performance metrics, because the exclusions are where the representation's boundaries become visible.

It matters because it is why dissent and standing are epistemic and not only political. Knowledge stays defeasible only if evidence the existing representation did not know how to recognize can still arrive — and it arrives through the people who carry it. That makes fallibilism material: a system is not meaningfully open to correction if the people who know it is wrong must exhaust themselves to prove it, which is the condition corrigibility rent prices.
entries.scope: M. Foundational Ethotechnic principles. The principles the method's laws and standards rest on.
operationalTests: Cases outside the model's support can enter as challenges rather than being discarded as noise.
Exception patterns feed category review, not only case resolution.
The cost of raising an excluded case is measured against the challenger's capacity to bear it.
entries.genealogy: The fallibilist premise under exception learning and safe incompleteness: the residual is data, and who can afford to bring it decides whether the institution can know.

minimumEvidence.artifact: An exceptions register where out-of-support cases are recorded as potential category evidence.
minimumEvidence.behavior: An excluded case that produced a category or rule review rather than a case-level fix.
minimumEvidence.metric: Share of exception classes whose pattern reached a category or rule review.

entries.title: Feedback proximity
entries.bodyHtml:
The design principle that the causal distance between an institutional error and the actors who can revise the generating rule should be kept as short as the stakes demand. Where error-bearing parties sit far from rule-makers (by hierarchy, by time, by evidence format, or by classification), corrections arrive late, weakened, or not at all.

It matters because proximity is not visibility. A harm can be fully visible to the people carrying it and still reach nobody who can change the rule that produces it. Shortening proximity means building the channels that let mismatch travel from the edge back to the rule: corrective standing, records that travel, and halt stratification. Insulation keeps harm from reaching anyone who can change the rule; feedback proximity is the commitment to shorten the path.
entries.scope: M. Foundational Ethotechnic principles. The principles the method's laws and standards rest on.
operationalTests: A harm reported at the frontline reaches an actor who can change the generating rule through a bounded number of named hops.
The latency from first signal to rule revision is measured and bounded, not merely visible.
Error-bearing parties can state the shortest path from their report to a rule change, and that path exists.
entries.genealogy: The positive form of insulation: where insulation keeps harm from reaching anyone who can change the rule, feedback proximity names the design commitment to shorten that path.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A mapped path from frontline signal to rule-revising authority, with named responders at each hop.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A reported mismatch that produced a rule change without an intervening heroic intervention.
minimumEvidence.metric: Time, or number of hops, from first signal to generating-rule revision, tracked per failure class.

entries.title: Asymmetric-capacity restraint
entries.bodyHtml:
The principle that an institution's obligations to remain contestable and revisable grow with its capacity to classify, monitor, automate, enforce, and scale. The more a system can see, sort, act on, and impose its categories, the stronger the counterweights must be.

It matters because capacity is not neutral. A system that can classify at scale can misclassify at scale, and a system that can enforce quickly can commit quickly. Restraint is the obligation side of capability overhang: capability may expand only as fast as the correction obligation that checks it. It is why earned autonomy is conditional rather than cumulative, and it makes Law XI's burden normative: every expansion of capacity carries a proportional expansion of contestation and revision.
entries.scope: M. Foundational Ethotechnic principles. The principles the method's laws and standards rest on.
operationalTests: Each expansion of classification, monitoring, or enforcement capacity is paired with a stated increase in contestation and revision capacity.
Correction capacity grows with authority, and the pairing is recorded rather than asserted.
A capability that outruns its correction capacity is refused admission or narrowed, not shipped and apologized for later.
entries.genealogy: The normative form of capability overhang: where overhang describes the mismatch, restraint names the obligation that prevents it.

minimumEvidence.artifact: A grant whose scope expansion is paired with a corresponding correction-capacity expansion, recorded in the same transition.
minimumEvidence.behavior: A capability refused or narrowed because its correction capacity was not yet provisioned.
minimumEvidence.metric: Ratio of correction capacity to granted authority, required non-decreasing across expansions.

entries.title: Principle of non-expropriation of resilience
entries.bodyHtml:
An institution may not use people's endurance as a permanent substitute for fixing its own failures. If it does, it loses the justification for asking them to endure. People's capacity to persevere through difficulty is real and valuable. It does not give an institution a claim on that endurance to keep a defective system running.

The principle sets a limit that resilience engineering's descriptions do not. That people adapt under pressure does not justify an institution relying on their adaptation. The principle is the test for whether an institution's results come from intrinsic performance or from unrecorded work by the people around the system.
entries.scope: M. Foundational Ethotechnic principles. The principles the method's laws and standards rest on.
operationalTests: Post-incident reviews classify heroic compensation by staff as a structural defect, not as a control that worked.
Workload modeling shows the system's operating pace stays sustainable when uncredited human workarounds are withdrawn.

minimumEvidence.behavior: Management halts system throughput expansion when error absorption by frontline staff exceeds defined thresholds.
minimumEvidence.metric: Ratio of compensated workarounds to structural defect tickets resolved in core workflows.
